17.title: The Burden against Damascus
17.context: A prophecy against Damascus: it will no longer be a city but a heap of ruins, and the fortified cities of Ephraim will be abandoned; the glory of Jacob will wane like a harvested field, and in that day people will look to their Maker and turn their eyes to the Holy One of Israel.

17.title: The Enemy Nations Are Defeated
17.context: Woe to the many nations that rage like the raging sea and roar like great waters; Yahweh rebukes them and they flee, driven like chaff before the wind; in the evening, sudden terror — before the morning, they are gone. This is the portion of those who loot us.

18.title: A Message to Cush
18.context: A message to Cush, the land of whirring wings beyond its rivers, which sends envoys by sea in papyrus boats; Yahweh says he will watch quietly from his dwelling place until the harvest, when he cuts off the shoots; at that time gifts will be brought to Yahweh of hosts at Mount Zion, the place of his Name.

19.title: The Burden against Egypt
19.context: An oracle on Egypt: Yahweh will judge it, its idols will tremble, the Nile dry up and its wise men be confused; yet in that day Egypt will turn to Yahweh and be blessed together with Assyria and Israel.

20.title: A Sign against Egypt and Cush
20.context: In the year the Assyrian commander-in-chief captures Ashdod, Yahweh tells Isaiah to take off his sackcloth and sandals and go stripped and barefoot for three years, a sign that the king of Assyria will lead away Egyptian and Cushite captives, so that those who looked to them for help will be dismayed.

21.title: Babylon Is Fallen
21.context: An oracle on the desert by the sea: the prophet sees a dreadful vision, and a watchman announces that Babylon has fallen and all its idols lie shattered.

21.title: The Burden against Edom
21.context: An oracle on Dumah (Edom): someone asks the watchman how much of the night is left, and he answers that morning is coming, but also night.

21.title: The Burden against Arabia
21.context: A prophecy against Arabia: caravans of Dedanites camp in the thickets of Arabia, and the people of Tema bring water for the thirsty and food for the fugitives, for they flee from the sword, the bent bow and the heat of battle; within a year, as a hired worker would count it, all the splendor of Kedar will come to an end, for Yahweh, the God of Israel, has spoken.

22.title: The Valley of Vision
22.context: An oracle on the Valley of Vision (Jerusalem): under threat the people do not look to God but throw a feast, reasoning that since they will die tomorrow they may as well eat and drink today.

22.title: A Message for Shebna
22.context: Yahweh rebukes the palace steward Shebna for carving himself a grand tomb and will replace him with Eliakim, placing the key of David’s house on his shoulder — an image Revelation 3:7 takes up.

23.title: The Burden against Tyre
23.context: A prophecy against Tyre: wail, you ships of Tarshish, for Tyre is destroyed and left without house or harbor; Yahweh of hosts planned it to bring low all the pride of glory. After seventy years Yahweh will deal with Tyre again, and her profits will be set apart for Yahweh.

24.title: God’s Judgment on the Earth
24.context: Yahweh will judge the whole earth, for its people have broken his laws and the everlasting covenant; in the end Yahweh will reign on Mount Zion in glory.

25.title: Praise to the Victorious God
25.context: The prophet praises Yahweh, a refuge for the poor; on Mount Zion he will prepare a feast for all peoples, remove the shroud over the nations, swallow up death and wipe away tears — hopes taken up in 1 Corinthians 15:54 and Revelation 21:4.

25.title: God Spreads a Feast for All Peoples
25.context: On this mountain Yahweh of hosts will prepare a feast of rich food for all peoples; he will destroy the shroud that covers all peoples, and swallow up death forever. The Lord Yahweh will wipe away the tears from all faces; Paul quotes verse 8 in 1 Corinthians 15:54 and Revelation 7:17; 21:4 echoes it.

25.title: God Will Punish Moab
25.context: Yahweh’s hand will rest on this mountain; but Moab will be trampled down in his place as straw is trampled down in the manure pit.

26.title: A Song of Salvation
26.context: In that day Judah will sing of a strong city with salvation as its walls; Yahweh keeps in perfect peace those whose minds are steadfast because they trust in him, so they should trust him forever.

26.title: Judgment and Restoration
26.context: Yahweh tells his people to hide in their rooms for a little while until his wrath passes, for he is coming to punish the earth’s sin and the serpent Leviathan.

28.title: The Captivity of Ephraim
28.context: Woe to the proud wreath of the drunkards of Ephraim: it will be trampled underfoot; but in that day Yahweh of hosts will be a glorious crown for the remnant of his people, a spirit of justice to those who sit in judgment and strength to those who turn back the battle at the gate.

28.title: Isaiah and Judah's Drunken Prophets
28.context: Priests and prophets reel with drink and mock Isaiah’s message as childish babble, so Yahweh will speak to them through foreign tongues; Paul cites this in 1 Corinthians 14:21.

28.title: A Cornerstone in Zion
28.context: The rulers think their pact with death will protect them, but Yahweh lays in Zion a tested, precious cornerstone, and whoever trusts in it will not panic; Romans 9:33 and 1 Peter 2:6 quote it.

28.title: Listen and Hear
28.context: A farmer plows, sows and threshes each crop in the way that suits it; his God instructs him and teaches him the right way. All this also comes from Yahweh of hosts, wonderful in counsel and magnificent in wisdom.

29.title: Woe to David’s City
29.context: Woe to Ariel, the city where David camped: Yahweh will besiege it, and her voice will speak like a ghost from the ground; yet the hordes of her enemies will become like fine dust, and suddenly Yahweh of hosts will come with thunder, earthquake and a consuming flame.

29.title: No One Heeds the Warning
29.context: The people are spiritually stupefied, the vision sealed to them like a closed scroll; they honor God with their lips while their hearts are far from him — words Jesus quotes in Matthew 15:8–9.

29.title: Sanctification for the Godly
29.context: Woe to those who go to great depths to hide their plans from Yahweh and ask, “Who sees us?” In that day the deaf will hear the words of the scroll and the eyes of the blind will see; the humble will rejoice in Yahweh, and the people will honor his name and stand in awe of the God of Israel.

30.title: The Worthless Treaty with Egypt
30.context: “Woe to the obstinate children,” declares Yahweh, who carry out plans that are not his and form an alliance without his Spirit; they go down to Egypt without consulting him, but Egypt’s protection will become their shame.

30.title: A Disobedient People
30.context: Yahweh has Isaiah write down a record of the people’s rebellion: they refuse his instruction and tell the prophets to speak only pleasant things.

30.title: God Will Be Gracious
30.context: Yahweh will be gracious to Zion’s people when they cry out; they will hear a voice behind them saying, “This is the way; walk in it,” throw away their idols and enjoy abundant harvests.

30.title: God Will Punish Assyria
30.context: See, the Name of Yahweh comes from afar, with burning anger and dense clouds of smoke; his lips are full of wrath and his tongue is a consuming fire, and his breath is like a rushing torrent. Assyria will be terrified at Yahweh’s voice, and there will be singing like the night you celebrate a holy festival.

31.title: Woe to Those Who Rely on Egypt
31.context: Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help, who rely on horses and trust in chariots, but do not look to the Holy One of Israel or seek help from Yahweh; the Egyptians are mortals and not God, their horses are flesh and not spirit. Yahweh will come down like a lion and defend Jerusalem like birds hovering overhead.

32.title: A Righteous King
32.context: See, a king will reign in righteousness and rulers will rule with justice; each one will be like a shelter from the wind and a refuge from the storm, like streams of water in the desert and the shadow of a great rock in a thirsty land.

32.title: The Women of Jerusalem
32.context: The prophet warns complacent women that city and fields will be laid waste until the Spirit is poured out from on high, the desert becomes fertile, and righteousness brings peace and security.

33.title: Yahweh Is Exalted
33.context: Woe to you, destroyer, who have not been destroyed! Yahweh, be gracious to us; we long for you. Yahweh is exalted, for he dwells on high; he will fill Zion with justice and righteousness, and the fear of Yahweh is the key to this treasure.

33.title: Yahweh's Warning to His Enemies
33.context: “Now will I arise,” says Yahweh; “now will I be exalted”; the peoples will be burned to ashes, thorns cut down and set ablaze. Sinners in Zion are terrified, and ask who can dwell with the consuming fire; the one who walks righteously and speaks what is right will dwell on the heights.

33.title: A Glorious Future
33.context: The people will see the king in his beauty, for Yahweh is their judge, lawgiver and king who will save them; no one in Zion will say they are sick, and their sins will be forgiven.

34.title: Judgment on the Nations
34.context: Come near, you nations, and listen; Yahweh is angry with all nations, and the heavens will be rolled up like a scroll. His sword descends in judgment on Edom, whose land will become burning pitch and desolate wasteland, for Yahweh has a day of vengeance, a year of retribution to uphold Zion’s cause.

35.title: The Glory of Zion
35.context: The wilderness will rejoice and blossom; the blind will see, the deaf hear, the lame leap and the mute sing, and on a Highway of Holiness the redeemed will return to Zion with singing. Jesus alludes to this in Matthew 11:5.

36.title: Sennacherib Threatens Jerusalem
36.context: Sennacherib captures Judah’s cities and sends his field commander to Jerusalem, who mocks Hezekiah’s trust in Yahweh and urges the people to surrender (parallel to 2 Kings 18–19).

37.title: Isaiah’s Message of Deliverance
37.context: Hezekiah goes to the temple in sackcloth and sends to Isaiah, who tells him not to fear: Yahweh will send the Assyrian king home to die by the sword.

37.title: Sennacherib’s Blasphemous Letter
37.context: The Assyrian king sends a threatening letter, and Hezekiah spreads it before Yahweh and prays, confessing that Yahweh alone is God over all kingdoms and asking him to save them so the world will know.

37.title: Sennacherib’s Fall Prophesied
37.context: Isaiah brings Yahweh’s answer that the Assyrian king will not enter the city; that night the angel of Yahweh strikes down 185,000 Assyrians, and Sennacherib withdraws to Nineveh, where his sons later kill him.

38.title: Hezekiah’s Illness and Recovery
38.context: Hezekiah becomes mortally ill and prays with tears; Yahweh adds fifteen years to his life, confirming it with the shadow’s retreat, and Hezekiah writes a song of thanks after he recovers.

39.title: Hezekiah Shows His Treasures
39.context: Envoys from Babylon visit, and Hezekiah shows them all his treasures; Isaiah foretells that everything will one day be carried off to Babylon.

40.title: Prepare the Way for Yahweh
40.context: “Comfort my people”: Jerusalem’s hard service is over and her sin pardoned; a voice calls to prepare the way for Yahweh; people are like grass but God’s word stands forever; Yahweh will tend his flock like a shepherd. The Gospels apply the voice to John the Baptist (Matthew 3:3).

40.title: The God of Israel Has No Equal
40.context: Who can measure the heavens or compare with God? The nations are like a drop in a bucket and idols are made by craftsmen; Yahweh is the everlasting God and Creator who never grows weary, and those who wait for him renew their strength and soar like eagles.

41.title: God’s Help to Israel
41.context: Yahweh summons the nations to court and raises up a conqueror from the east; to Israel his servant he says not to fear, for he is with them, will strengthen and help them and uphold them with his righteous right hand.

41.title: Meaningless Idols
41.context: Yahweh challenges the idols to foretell the future and show what power they have; they can do nothing, and those who choose them are detestable.

42.title: Here Is My Servant
42.context: “Here is my servant,” chosen and delighted in by God, on whom he puts his Spirit to bring justice to the nations; he will not shout, will not break a bruised reed or snuff out a smoldering wick. Matthew 12:17–21 applies this to Jesus.

42.title: A New Song of Praise
42.context: Sing to Yahweh a new song, his praise from the ends of the earth, you who go down to the sea, you islands and all who live in them; Yahweh will march out like a champion, like a warrior he will stir up his zeal, and will triumph over his enemies.

42.title: God Promises to Help His People
42.context: Yahweh says he has long been silent but will now cry out like a woman in labor; he will lead the blind on unfamiliar paths, turn darkness into light, and shame those who trust in idols.

42.title: Israel Is Deaf and Blind
42.context: Yahweh rebukes Israel, his servant, for being deaf and blind, seeing much but not paying attention; they are plundered because they sinned against him and would not walk in his ways.

43.title: Israel’s Only Savior
43.context: Yahweh tells Israel not to fear, for he has redeemed and called them by name — they are his; when they pass through waters or fire he will be with them, for he is Yahweh their God, their Savior.

43.title: Israel Is Yahweh's Witness
43.context: Yahweh calls Israel to be his witnesses that before him no god was formed and none will come after; he alone is Yahweh, and apart from him there is no savior.

43.title: A Way in the Wilderness
43.context: Yahweh will act against Babylon for Israel’s sake; he tells them not to dwell on the past, for he is doing a new thing, making a way in the wilderness and rivers in the desert.

43.title: Israel’s Unfaithfulness
43.context: Israel has not called on Yahweh but has wearied him with their sins; yet for his own sake he blots out their transgressions and remembers their sins no more.

44.title: Yahweh Has Chosen Israel
44.context: Yahweh promises to pour out his Spirit on Israel’s descendants like water on thirsty ground, and they will spring up like willows by flowing streams.

44.title: Worthless Idols
44.context: The idol-maker uses half a log to cook his food and warm himself and carves the other half into a god to bow down and pray to, never stopping to think that what he holds is a lie.

44.title: Jerusalem to Be Restored
44.context: Yahweh reminds Israel not to forget him, for he has swept away their sins and calls them to return; he declares that Jerusalem will be inhabited again and calls Cyrus his shepherd.

45.title: God Calls Cyrus
45.context: Yahweh calls Cyrus king of Persia his anointed, whom he will empower to subdue nations so that he may know the God of Israel summons him by name; though Cyrus does not know him, Yahweh uses him for Israel’s sake.

45.title: The Lord of Creation and History
45.context: Woe to those who quarrel with their Maker — does the clay say to the potter, “What are you making?” Yahweh made the earth and created mankind on it; his own hands stretched out the heavens. He raised up Cyrus in his righteousness to rebuild his city and set the exiles free, not for a price or reward.

45.title: The Lord of Heaven and Earth and Babylon's Idols
45.context: Yahweh calls the survivors of the nations: there is no God but him, and all the ends of the earth are to turn to him and be saved; he swears that every knee will bow to him and every tongue swear allegiance. Paul cites this in Romans 14:11 and Philippians 2:10–11.

47.title: The Humiliation of Babylon
47.context: Babylon must come down from her throne to sit in the dust; she thought she would be queen forever with no equal and relied on sorcery and astrologers, but disaster will strike suddenly and no one will save her.

48.title: Israel’s Stubbornness
48.context: Hear this, house of Jacob, you who take oaths in the name of Yahweh but not in truth or righteousness: because Israel is stubborn, Yahweh declared things beforehand so they could not credit idols; for his own name's sake he delays his wrath, refining them in the furnace of affliction, for the sake of his own glory.

48.title: Deliverance Promised to Israel
48.context: Yahweh declares that he is the first and the last, whose hand laid the earth’s foundations and spread out the heavens; through his chosen one he will act against Babylon, and he calls his people to leave it.

48.title: Yahweh's Plan for His People
48.context: Yahweh their Redeemer teaches them what is best; if only they had listened, their peace would have been like a river and their righteousness like the waves of the sea.

49.title: The Servant and Light to the Gentiles
49.context: The servant says Yahweh called him from the womb and made his mouth like a sharp sword; though he feels his labor is in vain, Yahweh will make him not only restore Israel but be a light to the nations, bringing salvation to the ends of the earth (cited in Luke 2:32 and Acts 13:47).

49.title: The Restoration of Jerusalem
49.context: In the time of favor Yahweh answers his servant to restore the land and free the captives; when Zion says Yahweh has forgotten her, he answers that a mother may forget her nursing child, but he will never forget Zion. Paul cites verse 8 in 2 Corinthians 6:2.

50.title: The Servant’s Obedience
50.context: The servant says Yahweh wakens his ear each morning so he can sustain the weary with a word; he did not turn back but offered his back to those who struck him and his face to mocking and spitting, and because Yahweh helps him he is not disgraced.

51.title: Salvation for Zion
51.context: Those who pursue righteousness should look to the rock from which they were cut — Abraham and Sarah; Yahweh will comfort Zion, make its wastelands like Eden, and his salvation will last forever.

51.title: God’s Fury Removed
51.context: Jerusalem has drunk the cup of Yahweh’s wrath, but now he takes it from her hand and gives it to those who tormented her.

52.title: Deliverance for Jerusalem
52.context: Zion is to awake, put on beautiful garments and shake off her chains; how beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news that God reigns; the people are to leave Babylon, with Yahweh going before them.

52.title: The Servant Exalted
52.context: The fourth Servant Song (52:13–53:12): the servant is despised, wounded for our sins and silent like a lamb led to slaughter; his life becomes an offering that makes many righteous, and he is finally exalted. The New Testament applies it to Jesus (Matthew 8:17; Acts 8:32–35; 1 Peter 2:22–25).

54.title: Future Blessings for Zion
54.context: The barren woman is to sing, for her children will outnumber those of the married wife; her Maker Yahweh is her husband, who abandoned her briefly but will gather her with everlasting love. Paul cites this in Galatians 4:27.

54.title: The Future of Jerusalem
54.context: The storm-battered city will be rebuilt with precious stones, its children taught by Yahweh and enjoying great peace, and no weapon formed against it will succeed. Jesus cites verse 13 in John 6:45.

55.title: Invitation to the Needy
55.context: Yahweh invites the thirsty to come and eat and drink without cost and offers an everlasting covenant; seek him while he may be found, let the wicked turn to him for abundant pardon, for his thoughts are higher than ours and his word will not return empty.

56.title: Salvation for Foreigners
56.context: Yahweh calls for justice and righteousness, for his salvation is near; foreigners and eunuchs who hold fast to his covenant will be welcomed, and his house will be called a house of prayer for all nations, as Jesus quotes in Mark 11:17.

56.title: Israel’s Sinful Leaders
56.context: All you beasts of the field, come and devour; Israel’s watchmen are blind, they all lack knowledge; they are all mute dogs, they cannot bark, lazy and fond of sleep. They are shepherds who lack understanding; they all turn to their own way, they seek their own gain.

57.title: The Blessed Death of the Righteous
57.context: The righteous die and no one takes it to heart, yet they are taken away from coming evil into peace; meanwhile idolaters practice immorality and child sacrifice everywhere, having forgotten Yahweh.

57.title: Healing for the Repentant
57.context: The high and exalted One, who lives forever and whose name is holy, dwells in a high and holy place and also with the contrite and humble, to revive and heal them; but there is no peace for the wicked.

58.title: True Fasts and Sabbaths
58.context: Yahweh tells Isaiah to cry out against the people’s sin: they fast while quarreling and exploiting workers; the fast God wants is to loosen the chains of injustice, free the oppressed and share bread with the hungry, and then their light will break forth like the dawn.

58.title: Blessing for Those Who Keep the Sabbath
58.context: If they call the Sabbath a delight and honor Yahweh’s holy day rather than pursuing their own interests, they will find joy in Yahweh, and he will make them ride on the heights of the land.

59.title: Sin Separates Us from God
59.context: It is not that Yahweh’s arm is too short to save, but that their sins have separated them from God; their hands are stained with blood and their lips speak lies. Paul quotes some lines in Romans 3:15–17.

59.title: The People Confess Their Sin
59.context: The people confess that justice is far from them; they hope for light but find darkness, their offenses multiply before God, and truth stumbles in the streets.

59.title: The Covenant of the Redeemer
59.context: Seeing no one to intervene, Yahweh brings salvation himself, putting on righteousness as a breastplate and salvation as a helmet; the Redeemer will come to Zion to those who turn from sin, and his Spirit and word will never depart from them.

60.title: Future Glory for Zion
60.context: Zion is to arise and shine, for the glory of Yahweh rises on her; nations and kings will come to her light, her gates will always be open, and Yahweh will be her everlasting light — images Revelation 21:23–25 takes up.

61.title: The Year of Yahweh’s Favor
61.context: The Spirit of Yahweh is on the anointed one, sent to bring good news to the poor, bind up the brokenhearted, proclaim freedom for captives and announce the year of Yahweh’s favor. Jesus reads this in the Nazareth synagogue and says it is fulfilled that day (Luke 4:16–21).

63.title: God’s Vengeance on the Nations
63.context: A figure in crimson comes from Edom, having trodden the winepress alone, his garments stained, for the day of vengeance and the year of redemption have come — an image Revelation 19:13–15 takes up.

63.title: God’s Mercies Recalled
63.context: The prophet recalls Yahweh’s kindness: in all his people’s distress he too was distressed, and in love he redeemed them; but they rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit, and then remembered the days of Moses.

63.title: A Prayer for Mercy
63.context: The prayer asks Yahweh to look down from heaven — he is their Father and Redeemer — and pleads that he would tear open the heavens and come down, making the mountains tremble.

65.title: Judgments and Promises
65.context: Yahweh says he was found by those who did not seek him while he held out his hands all day to a rebellious people; he will judge the idolaters but spare his servants. Paul cites this in Romans 10:20–21.

65.title: A New Heaven and a New Earth
65.context: Yahweh will create new heavens and a new earth, and former things will not be remembered; Jerusalem will be a joy with no more weeping, people will live long and secure, and the wolf will feed with the lamb — a hope taken up in 2 Peter 3:13 and Revelation 21:1.

66.title: Heaven Is My Throne
66.context: Yahweh says heaven is his throne and earth his footstool, so what house could be built for him? He esteems the humble and contrite who tremble at his word; he will extend peace to Jerusalem like a river, and all peoples will come to worship. Stephen quotes this in Acts 7:49–50.

1.title: Jeremiah Is Called
1.context: Yahweh tells Jeremiah that he knew him and set him apart before he was born, appointing him a prophet to the nations; when Jeremiah protests that he is too young, Yahweh puts his words in his mouth and sends him to uproot and to build.

1.title: Two Visions
1.context: Two visions: an almond branch (in Hebrew a play on “watching”) showing Yahweh is watching to see his word fulfilled, and a boiling pot tilting from the north, showing disaster will pour out on Judah from there.

2.title: Israel Has Forsaken God
2.context: Yahweh recalls Israel’s early devotion, when she followed him through the wilderness as a bride, holy to him, and anyone who harmed her was held guilty.

2.title: The Sins of Israel's Ancestors
2.context: The priests, those who handle the law, the shepherds and the prophets turned away from Yahweh; and his people committed two sins: they have forsaken him, the spring of living water, and dug their own cisterns, broken cisterns that cannot hold water.

2.title: God Accuses His People
2.context: Yahweh brings a charge against his people for doing what no nation has done: abandoning him, the spring of living water, and digging for themselves broken cisterns that cannot hold water.

2.title: The Consequence of Israel’s Sin
2.context: Is Israel a servant, a slave by birth? Why then has he become plunder? Lions have roared; this is something Israel brought on himself by forsaking Yahweh while he led them in the way; why go to Egypt to drink from the Nile or to Assyria to drink from the Euphrates?

2.title: Israel’s Unfaithfulness
2.context: Long ago you broke off your yoke, saying “I will not serve you!” Yet on every hill and under every tree you lay down as a prostitute; Yahweh had planted a choice vine, but it turned into a wild one — even with lye and soap, the stain of guilt remains.

2.title: Israel Deserves Punishment
2.context: As a thief is disgraced when caught, so the house of Israel — kings, officials, priests and prophets — is disgraced; they say to wood, “You are my father,” and to stone, “You gave me birth,” yet in trouble they cry, “Come and save us!” Where are the gods they made?

3.title: The Wages of the Harlot
3.context: If a man divorces his wife and she marries another, may he return to her? Israel has lived as a prostitute with many lovers, and yet Yahweh calls, “Return to me”; the rains have been withheld because of her adultery.

3.title: Judah Follows Israel’s Example
3.context: In Josiah’s time Yahweh notes that Judah saw Israel sent away for unfaithfulness yet still only pretended to return; he calls the faithless children to come back and promises them shepherds after his own heart.

3.title: God's People Worship Idols
3.context: Yahweh longed for Israel to call him Father and never turn away, but they betrayed him like an unfaithful wife; at last the people confess their shame and return to Yahweh.

4.title: A Plea to Return
4.context: Yahweh urges Israel, if they return, to remove their detestable idols, break up their unplowed ground and cleanse their hearts, lest his wrath break out.

4.title: Disaster from the North
4.context: Announce in Judah and proclaim in Jerusalem: blow the trumpet and flee to the fortified cities, for disaster and great destruction are coming from the north; a lion has come out of his lair, a destroyer of nations, to make the land a ruin. Put on sackcloth and mourn, for the fierce anger of Yahweh has not turned away.

4.title: Judah Besieged by the Enemy
4.context: The enemy advances like clouds and a whirlwind, horses swifter than eagles; Jerusalem must wash the evil from its heart to be saved.

4.title: Lamentation for Judah
4.context: Hearing the trumpet and the alarm of war, the prophet is in anguish, for his people are foolish, skilled in doing evil but not in doing good.

4.title: Jeremiah's Vision of Coming Destruction
4.context: Jeremiah sees the earth formless and empty and the heavens without light, mountains quaking and cities in ruins, like creation undone; yet Yahweh says he will not make a complete end.

5.title: No One Is Just
5.context: Yahweh says that if one person can be found in Jerusalem’s streets who acts justly and seeks truth, he will pardon the city; but rich and poor alike refuse to repent.

5.title: Judgment Proclaimed
5.context: The people deny that Yahweh will bring disaster and dismiss the prophets as wind; so Yahweh makes his words fire in Jeremiah’s mouth and brings a distant nation against them.

5.title: God Warns His People
5.context: Yahweh set the sea’s boundary and sends rain in season, yet the people do not fear him; scoundrels trap others, prophets speak lies, and the people love it so.

6.title: Jerusalem’s Final Warning
6.context: The people of Benjamin are told to flee Jerusalem, for disaster looms from the north; Yahweh calls the enemy to besiege the city because it is full of oppression.

6.title: Rebellious Israel
6.context: The people’s ears are closed and they cannot listen; from prophet to priest all deal falsely, treating the wound lightly and saying “Peace” when there is no peace.

6.title: Israel Rejects God's Way
6.context: Yahweh tells them to stand at the crossroads, ask for the ancient paths and walk in the good way to find rest for their souls; but they refuse to walk in it or heed the watchmen’s trumpet.

6.title: An Invasion from the North
6.context: A cruel people comes from the north with bow and spear, roaring like the sea; Yahweh makes Jeremiah a tester of metals, and the people prove to be rejected silver.

7.title: Jeremiah’s Message at the Temple Gate
7.context: At the temple gate Jeremiah warns the people not to trust in slogans about the temple; if they oppress foreigners, orphans and widows, this house will be destroyed like Shiloh. Jesus cites verse 11 when he clears the temple (Matthew 21:13).

7.title: Judah’s Idolatry Persists
7.context: Yahweh tells Jeremiah not to pray for the people, for whole families bake cakes for the Queen of Heaven and pour out offerings to other gods; what Yahweh wants is obedience, not sacrifice alone.

7.title: The Valley of Slaughter
7.context: Judah burns its children at Topheth in the Valley of Ben Hinnom, so Yahweh says it will be called the Valley of Slaughter, and bodies will lie as food for birds and beasts.

8.title: Sin and Punishment
8.context: People who fall get up and those who stray turn back, but this people clings to rebellion; even the stork knows its seasons, yet they do not know Yahweh’s requirements, and scribes have handled the law falsely.

8.title: Jeremiah Weeps for His People
8.context: Jeremiah is overwhelmed with grief, wounded by his people’s wound, and asks whether there is no balm in Gilead and no physician there, since his people are not healed.

9.title: Jerusalem Cries for Help
9.context: Yahweh calls for mourning women to teach their daughters laments, for death has climbed in through the windows; he says not to boast in wisdom or wealth but in knowing Yahweh, as Paul quotes in 1 Corinthians 1:31.

10.title: The Sovereignty of God
10.context: The nations’ idols are carved from wood by craftsmen, like scarecrows in a cucumber field that cannot speak or walk; but Yahweh is the true God, the living God and eternal King.

10.title: A Hymn of Praise to God
10.context: Yahweh made the earth by his power and founded the world by his wisdom; idol worshippers are senseless, but the Portion of Jacob is not like them, for he is the Maker of all things.

10.title: The Coming Captivity of Judah
10.context: Yahweh will hurl the land’s people out; the prophet admits that a person’s life is not their own to direct and asks Yahweh to correct with justice, not anger, and pour his wrath on the nations that do not know him.

11.title: The Broken Covenant
11.context: Yahweh reminds Judah of the covenant he made when he brought their ancestors out of Egypt, but they have refused to listen like their fathers; their gods are as many as their towns, so disaster will come.

11.title: A Plot against Jeremiah
11.context: Jeremiah is like a gentle lamb led to slaughter, unaware that the men of Anathoth are plotting against him; Yahweh reveals the plot and promises to punish them.

12.title: The Prosperity of the Wicked
12.context: Jeremiah asks Yahweh why the way of the wicked prospers; Yahweh answers that if racing against men on foot has worn him out, how will he compete with horses?

12.title: God’s Answer to Jeremiah
12.context: Yahweh says he has forsaken his house and handed the one he loves to her enemies; many shepherds have ruined his vineyard.

12.title: A Message for Israel’s Neighbors
12.context: Yahweh will uproot the neighbors who attacked Israel, but if they diligently learn his people’s ways, they too will be established among them.

13.title: The Linen Loincloth
13.context: Jeremiah buys a linen belt and hides it in a rock crevice by the Euphrates; when he retrieves it, it is ruined, and Yahweh says he will ruin Judah’s pride the same way.

13.title: The Wineskins
13.context: Every wineskin should be filled with wine; Yahweh says he will fill the land’s people with drunkenness and smash them against one another.

13.title: Captivity Threatened
13.context: Yahweh urges them to give him glory before darkness falls; can an Ethiopian change his skin or a leopard its spots? Neither can those accustomed to evil do good.

14.title: Drought, Famine, Sword, and Plague
14.context: Drought strikes Judah, cisterns run dry and the ground cracks; the people confess and plead, but Yahweh refuses them and says the prophets promising no sword or famine are lying.

14.title: A Prayer for Mercy
14.context: The people plead again: has Yahweh utterly rejected Judah? They confess their sin and ask him not to break his covenant, for the sake of his name; can any idol of the nations bring rain?

15.title: Judgment to Continue
15.context: Yahweh says that even if Moses and Samuel stood before him he would not relent toward this people, because of what King Manasseh did; sword, dogs, birds and beasts will come upon them.

15.title: Jeremiah’s Woe
15.context: Jeremiah laments being born a man of strife; he found Yahweh’s words and ate them with joy, yet suffers alone; Yahweh promises that if he returns, he will make him a fortified bronze wall.

16.title: Disaster Predicted
16.context: Yahweh tells Jeremiah not to marry or have children and not to enter houses of mourning or feasting, as a sign that the people will die with no one to mourn or bury them.

16.title: God Will Restore Israel
16.context: A day is coming when people will no longer swear by Yahweh who brought Israel out of Egypt, but by Yahweh who brought them back from the land of the north.

16.title: The Punishment to Come
16.context: Yahweh will send many fishermen and hunters to search out the people from every hiding place, for his eyes see all their sins, and he will repay them double.

16.title: Jeremiah's Prayer of Trust
16.context: Jeremiah calls Yahweh his strength, fortress and refuge; nations will come from the ends of the earth to admit that their ancestors inherited only worthless idols.

17.title: The Sin and Punishment of Judah
17.context: Judah’s sin is engraved with an iron tool and diamond point on their hearts and on the horns of their altars; because of it they will lose their inheritance and serve enemies in a strange land.

17.title: A Collection of Sayings
17.context: Cursed is the one who trusts in man, like a bush in the desert; blessed is the one who trusts in Yahweh, like a tree planted by water; the heart is deceitful above all things, but Yahweh searches it.

17.title: Jeremiah’s Prayer for Deliverance
17.context: Jeremiah asks Yahweh to heal and save him, for Yahweh is his praise; he has not run from being a shepherd, and he asks that his persecutors be put to shame.

17.title: Restoring the Sabbath
17.context: Yahweh sends Jeremiah to the city gates to tell the people not to carry loads on the Sabbath; if they obey, David’s throne will endure, but if not, fire will consume the gates.

18.title: The Potter and the Clay
18.context: At the potter’s house Jeremiah sees a marred vessel reshaped into another; Yahweh says Israel is like clay in his hand, and he may relent or not depending on whether a nation turns from evil.

18.title: The People Forget Yahweh
18.context: Yahweh says even the snow of Lebanon does not leave its crags, yet his people have forgotten him and burned incense to worthless idols, making their land a horror.

18.title: Another Plot against Jeremiah
18.context: The people plot to attack Jeremiah with their words, so he prays to Yahweh, reminding him that he once interceded for them and asking him to judge those who plot against him.

19.title: The Broken Jar
19.context: Jeremiah takes the elders to the Valley of Ben Hinnom and smashes a clay jar before them, announcing that Yahweh will shatter this people and city because they burned their children there as offerings to Baal.

20.title: Pashhur Persecutes Jeremiah
20.context: The priest Pashhur beats Jeremiah and puts him in stocks; when he is released the next day, Jeremiah says Yahweh renames Pashhur “Terror on Every Side” and he and his household will go into exile in Babylon.

20.title: Jeremiah’s Complaint
20.context: Jeremiah says Yahweh persuaded him and now he is mocked all day; he tries not to speak Yahweh’s name, but it is like fire shut up in his bones; he curses the day he was born.

21.title: Jerusalem Will Fall to Babylon
21.context: King Zedekiah sends to ask Yahweh for a miracle to drive Babylon away; Jeremiah replies that Yahweh himself will fight against the city and sets before the people the way of life — surrender to Babylon — and the way of death.

21.title: A Message to the House of David
21.context: Yahweh tells the house of David to administer justice every morning and rescue the robbed from the oppressor, lest his wrath break out like fire.

22.title: A Warning to Judah’s Kings
22.context: Yahweh sends Jeremiah to the palace to say that if the king does justice and does not oppress foreigners, orphans and widows, David’s line will continue on the throne; otherwise the palace will become a ruin.

22.title: A Warning about Shallum
22.context: Do not weep for the dead king (Josiah); weep for Shallum (Jehoahaz), who has been taken away, for he will die in exile and never return.

22.title: A Warning about Jehoiakim
22.context: Jehoiakim builds his palace by injustice and does not pay his workers; his father Josiah defended the poor and needy, which is what it means to know Yahweh, but Jehoiakim will be buried like a donkey dragged outside the gates.

22.title: The Fate of Jerusalem's People
22.context: Jerusalem is told to go up to Lebanon and cry out, for all her allies are crushed; she would not listen in her prosperity, and has been this way since her youth.

22.title: A Warning to Coniah
22.context: Yahweh says that even if Coniah (Jehoiachin) were a signet ring on his right hand, he would pull him off and hand him to Babylon; none of his offspring will sit on David’s throne.

23.title: David’s Righteous Branch
23.context: Yahweh condemns the shepherds who scatter his flock and promises to gather the remnant himself and raise up for David a righteous Branch who will reign wisely and do justice; he will be called “Yahweh Our Righteousness.”

23.title: Lying Prophets
23.context: Prophets and priests are godless; the false prophets speak visions from their own minds and promise peace to those who despise Yahweh, but Yahweh’s word is like fire and like a hammer that breaks rock.

23.title: False Prophecies
23.context: The people and prophets glibly talk about “the burden of Yahweh,” so Yahweh forbids the phrase, for each person’s own word has become their burden.

24.title: The Good and Bad Figs
24.context: Yahweh shows Jeremiah two baskets of figs, one very good and one very bad; the good represent the exiles in Babylon, whom he will give a heart to know him, and the bad represent Zedekiah and those left behind.

25.title: Seventy Years of Captivity
25.context: Jeremiah has preached for twenty-three years without being heard; Yahweh will make the land desolate and the nations will serve Babylon for seventy years, after which Babylon too will be punished. Daniel reads of these seventy years in Daniel 9:2.

25.title: The Cup of God’s Wrath
25.context: Yahweh has Jeremiah make the nations drink the cup of his wrath, starting with Jerusalem and going on to Egypt, Philistia, Edom, Moab and others, and finally Babylon (Sheshach).

26.title: A Warning to the Cities of Judah
26.context: Jeremiah warns in the temple courts that it will become like Shiloh unless they repent; priests and prophets demand his death, but the officials and the people say he should not die, and elders cite Micah’s example; another prophet, Uriah, is killed by Jehoiakim.

27.title: The Yoke of Nebuchadnezzar
27.context: Wearing a yoke on his neck, Jeremiah announces that Yahweh has given the nations to Nebuchadnezzar and those who submit to Babylon will remain in their land; they must not believe prophets who say the temple articles will soon return.

28.title: Hananiah’s False Prophecy
28.context: The prophet Hananiah claims Yahweh will break Babylon’s yoke within two years and breaks the wooden yoke off Jeremiah’s neck; Yahweh says it will be replaced with iron, and Hananiah dies that same year.

29.title: Jeremiah’s Letter to the Exiles
29.context: Jeremiah writes to the exiles: build houses, plant gardens, marry and seek the welfare of the city where they live; after seventy years Yahweh will bring them back, for his plans for them are for peace and hope, and if they seek him wholeheartedly they will find him.

29.title: The Message to Shemaiah
29.context: Shemaiah, among the exiles, writes urging the priests to restrain Jeremiah; Yahweh says Shemaiah has preached rebellion, and neither he nor his descendants will see the good Yahweh will do.

30.title: The Restoration of Israel and Judah
30.context: Yahweh tells Jeremiah to write in a book that he will bring back the captives of Israel and Judah; it is a time of trouble for Jacob, but he will be saved from it, and they will serve David their king.

31.title: Mourning Turned to Joy
31.context: Yahweh loves Israel with an everlasting love and will build her again, and she will dance with tambourines; he will gather the blind, the lame and expectant mothers and lead them on a level path beside streams.

31.title: Yahweh Has Compassion on Israel
31.context: Rachel weeps for her children and refuses comfort (quoted in Matthew 2:18); Yahweh tells her to stop weeping, for her children will return from the enemy’s land; Ephraim repents, and Yahweh has compassion on him.

31.title: The New Covenant
31.context: Yahweh promises a new covenant with Israel and Judah, unlike the one made at the exodus: he will write his law on their hearts, all will know him, and he will forgive their sins and remember them no more. Hebrews 8:8–12 quotes it.

32.title: Jeremiah Buys Hanamel’s Field
32.context: During the siege, while confined in the courtyard of the guard, Jeremiah obeys Yahweh and buys his cousin Hanamel’s field at Anathoth, sealing the deeds in a clay jar as a sign that houses and fields will again be bought in this land.

32.title: Jeremiah Prays for Understanding
32.context: Jeremiah prays that nothing is too hard for Yahweh, recounts his deeds since the exodus, and wonders why he was told to buy a field as the city falls.

32.title: A Promise of Restoration
32.context: Yahweh answers that he will gather his people from all nations, give them one heart and one way, make an everlasting covenant with them so they fear him forever, and fields will again be bought and sold.

33.title: The Excellence of the Restored Nation
33.context: Yahweh invites Jeremiah to call on him and promises to reveal great things; he will heal the city, forgive its sins and restore the sounds of joy, and his covenant with David and the Levites is as firm as his covenant with day and night.

34.title: A Prophecy against Zedekiah
34.context: Yahweh tells Zedekiah that the city will be handed to Babylon and he will be taken captive, but he will die in peace and be mourned with burning of spices.

34.title: Freedom for Hebrew Slaves
34.context: During the siege the people make a covenant to free their Hebrew slaves, then take them back once the danger eases; Yahweh says that since they withheld freedom, he will “free” sword, plague and famine against them.

35.title: The Obedience of the Rechabites
35.context: Jeremiah offers the Rechabites wine in the temple, and they refuse because of their ancestor Jonadab’s command; Yahweh contrasts their obedience with Judah’s refusal to obey him and promises that their line will always serve him.

36.title: Jeremiah’s Scroll Read in the Temple
36.context: In Jehoiakim’s fourth year Yahweh tells Jeremiah to write his words on a scroll; Jeremiah dictates to Baruch, who reads it to the people at the temple on a fast day.

36.title: Jeremiah’s Scroll Read in the Palace
36.context: Micaiah reports the scroll to the officials, who have Baruch read it to them; alarmed, they decide to tell the king and urge Baruch and Jeremiah to hide.

36.title: Jehoiakim Burns the Scroll
36.context: Jehoiakim sits by a fire as the scroll is read, cutting off a few columns at a time and throwing them into the flames until it is gone; neither he nor his servants show any fear.

36.title: Jeremiah Rewrites the Scroll
36.context: Yahweh tells Jeremiah to write another scroll and declares that none of Jehoiakim’s line will sit on David’s throne; Baruch writes it again and adds many similar words.

37.title: Jeremiah Warns Zedekiah
37.context: Zedekiah asks Jeremiah to pray for them; when Egypt’s army advances, Babylon lifts the siege for a while, but Jeremiah says the Babylonians will return and burn the city.

37.title: Jeremiah Imprisoned
37.context: Heading for Benjamin, Jeremiah is accused of deserting to Babylon, beaten and kept in a dungeon for many days; Zedekiah secretly asks for a word from Yahweh, Jeremiah says he will be handed to Babylon, and the king moves him to the courtyard of the guard.

38.title: Jeremiah Cast into the Cistern
38.context: The officials accuse Jeremiah of discouraging the soldiers and lower him into a muddy cistern; the Cushite official Ebed-melech pleads with the king and pulls him out with ropes and old rags.

38.title: Zedekiah Consults Jeremiah
38.context: Zedekiah consults Jeremiah in secret, and Jeremiah urges him to surrender to Babylon so that the city will not be burned and he will live; the king fears the Jews and does not obey.

39.title: The Fall of Jerusalem
39.context: In Zedekiah’s eleventh year the city falls; he flees but is captured, watches his sons executed, is blinded and taken to Babylon; the walls are torn down and the people exiled, leaving only the poorest.

39.title: Jeremiah Delivered
39.context: Nebuchadnezzar orders the commander of the guard to treat Jeremiah well, so he is released from the courtyard and entrusted to Gedaliah to live among the people.

39.title: Ebed-melech's Hope
39.context: Yahweh promises Ebed-melech that because he trusted in Yahweh, he will not be handed over to those he fears on the day the city falls, but will escape with his life.

40.title: Jeremiah Remains in Judah
40.context: Nebuzaradan the commander frees Jeremiah at Ramah and lets him choose between Babylon and staying behind; Jeremiah chooses to remain in Judah with Gedaliah.

40.title: Gedaliah Governs in Judah
40.context: Babylon appoints Gedaliah governor of Judah, and the scattered army officers and people gather to him; he urges them to serve Babylon and harvest wine, summer fruit and oil.

40.title: The Plot against Gedaliah
40.context: Johanan warns Gedaliah that the Ammonite king has sent Ishmael to kill him and offers to strike first, but Gedaliah refuses to believe it.

42.title: A Warning against Going to Egypt
42.context: After Gedaliah’s murder, the army officers and people ask Jeremiah to seek Yahweh’s guidance for them, swearing they will obey whatever he says.

42.title: Yahweh Answers Jeremiah's Prayer
42.context: After ten days Yahweh answers that if they stay in the land he will build them up and they need not fear Babylon’s king, but if they insist on going to Egypt, the sword and famine they fear will overtake them there.

43.title: Jeremiah Taken to Egypt
43.context: Johanan and the others call Jeremiah a liar, disobey Yahweh and take the remnant, including Jeremiah and Baruch, to Tahpanhes in Egypt, where Jeremiah foretells that Nebuchadnezzar will strike Egypt.

44.title: Judgment on the Jews in Egypt
44.context: The Judeans in Egypt keep burning incense to the Queen of Heaven, claiming things went well when they did so; Jeremiah announces they will perish in Egypt and gives Pharaoh Hophra’s fall as a sign.

45.title: Jeremiah’s Message to Baruch
45.context: While writing the scroll, Baruch groans in weariness; Yahweh tells him not to seek great things for himself but promises to preserve his life wherever he goes.

46.title: Judgment on Egypt
46.context: On Egypt: Pharaoh Neco’s army is defeated by Nebuchadnezzar at Carchemish on the Euphrates; it is the day of vengeance of the Lord Yahweh of hosts, and Egypt has no healing.

46.title: Nebuchadnezzar Attacks
46.context: Yahweh foretells Nebuchadnezzar’s attack on Egypt; Egypt is like a beautiful heifer, but a gadfly comes from the north, and its gods and Pharaoh will be handed over.

46.title: Yahweh Will Save His People
46.context: Yahweh tells Jacob not to fear, for he will save them from afar; he will make an end of the nations but not of Jacob, whom he will discipline justly.

47.title: Judgment on the Philistines
47.context: On the Philistines: waters rising from the north will flood their land and cut off help for Tyre and Sidon; Yahweh’s sword cannot rest, for he has ordered it against Ashkelon and the coast.

48.title: Judgment on Moab
48.context: On Moab: Nebo and Kiriathaim are destroyed and Moab’s glory is gone; it trusted in its riches and in Chemosh, who will go into exile with his priests and officials.

48.title: Moab's Towns Are Destroyed
48.context: Moab has been at ease since youth, like wine left on its dregs and never poured out, so its taste is unchanged; now its towns are destroyed one by one and it will be ashamed of Chemosh.

48.title: Moab Will Be Humbled
48.context: Moab will be made drunk and mocked for its arrogance, as it once mocked Israel; yet the prophet weeps for Moab, which will be broken like an unwanted jar.

48.title: There Is No Escape for Moab
48.context: The enemy swoops like an eagle and Moab has no escape — whoever flees the terror falls into the pit; yet in the latter days Yahweh will restore Moab’s fortunes.

49.title: Judgment on the Ammonites
49.context: On Ammon: their god Malcam (Milcom) seized Gad’s land, so Yahweh will make Rabbah a ruin and Israel will reclaim its territory, though later he will restore the Ammonites.

49.title: Judgment on Edom
49.context: On Edom: its wisdom has vanished and Yahweh will strip Esau bare; it lives proudly in rocky clefts, but he will bring it down like Sodom and Gomorrah.

49.title: Judgment on Damascus
49.context: On Damascus: Hamath and Arpad are dismayed at bad news; Damascus grows feeble, its young men fall in the streets, and fire will consume Ben-hadad’s fortresses.

49.title: Judgment on Kedar and Hazor
49.context: On Kedar and the kingdoms of Hazor: Nebuchadnezzar will strike these eastern tent-dwelling peoples who live without gates or bars and seize their camels and herds.

49.title: Judgment on Elam
49.context: On Elam: Yahweh will break Elam’s bow and scatter its people to the four winds, yet in the latter days he will restore Elam’s fortunes.

50.title: A Prophecy against Babylon
50.context: Announce among the nations that Babylon is captured, Bel is put to shame and Marduk is terrified; a nation from the north will lay it waste.

50.title: Hope for Israel and Judah
50.context: In those days Israel and Judah together will come weeping to seek Yahweh, asking the way to Zion and joining him in an everlasting covenant; they had been lost sheep.

50.title: Babylon’s Fall Is Certain
50.context: Babylon rejoiced in plundering Yahweh’s inheritance, but now it will be shamed and become a wilderness; Yahweh will repay it as it has done.

50.title: Redemption for God’s People
50.context: Israel is a scattered flock, first devoured by Assyria and then crushed by Babylon; Yahweh will punish Babylon’s king, bring Israel back to its pasture and forgive the remnant.

50.title: The Destruction of Babylon
50.context: Yahweh summons armies against Babylon, which defied him; Israel’s Redeemer is strong — Yahweh of hosts is his name — and he will plead his people’s cause.

51.title: Judgment on Babylon
51.context: Yahweh will stir up a destroying wind against Babylon, once a golden cup in his hand that made the earth drunk but now suddenly fallen; he has roused the kings of the Medes to destroy it.

51.title: Praise to the God of Jacob
51.context: Yahweh made the earth by his power and founded the world by his wisdom; idol makers are senseless, but the Portion of Jacob is the Maker of all things (repeating 10:12–16).

51.title: Babylon’s Punishment
51.context: Yahweh calls Babylon his war club, with which he shattered nations, horses, rulers and governors.

51.title: Babylon Will Be Punished
51.context: Yahweh will repay Babylon for the wrong it did in Zion; this “destroying mountain” will be overthrown and left desolate forever, as nations prepare to attack it.

51.title: Yahweh Will Help Israel
51.context: Yahweh will plead Zion’s cause, dry up Babylon’s sea and make it a heap of ruins and a haunt of jackals, putting its people into a sleep from which they will not wake.

51.title: The Fate of Babylon
51.context: How Sheshach (Babylon) has been captured, the sea rising over it; Yahweh will punish Bel and make him spit out what he swallowed, and Babylon’s wall will fall.

51.title: A Message to the Israelites in Babylon
51.context: Yahweh calls those who escaped the sword to remember him from far away and keep Jerusalem in mind, though they were shamed when foreigners entered the sanctuary.

51.title: Babylon Is Destroyed
51.context: A cry rises from Babylon, for Yahweh is destroying it; its thick walls will be leveled and its high gates set on fire.

51.title: Jeremiah’s Message to Seraiah
51.context: Jeremiah writes Babylon’s doom on a scroll and gives it to Seraiah, Zedekiah’s officer, who is to read it in Babylon, tie a stone to it and throw it into the Euphrates as a sign that Babylon will sink in the same way.

52.title: The Fall of Jerusalem Recounted
52.context: An account of Jerusalem’s fall: Zedekiah does evil, the city is besieged until his eleventh year, famine breaks it, and the king flees, is captured, blinded at Riblah and taken to Babylon (parallel to 2 Kings 24–25).

52.title: The Temple Destroyed
52.context: Nebuzaradan, commander of the guard, burns Yahweh’s temple, the palace and the great houses, tears down the walls and breaks up the bronze pillars, the bronze sea and other temple furnishings to carry to Babylon.

52.title: Captives Carried to Babylon
52.context: The chief priests and officials are executed at Riblah, the numbers of the exiles are recorded, and finally Jehoiachin is released from prison in Babylon and eats at the king’s table for the rest of his life.

1.title: How Lonely Lies the City!
1.context: The first acrostic lament after Jerusalem’s fall: the city sits alone like a widow, weeping at night with no one to comfort her; she admits she is punished for her own sin and that Yahweh is righteous.

2.title: God’s Anger over Jerusalem
2.context: The second lament describes Yahweh in anger acting like an enemy against Zion, its temple and walls; children faint in the streets and prophets saw only false visions; the poet urges the people to pour out their hearts to the Lord at night.

3.title: The Prophet’s Afflictions
3.context: The poet speaks of his own suffering, as if walled in darkness; then he recalls that Yahweh’s steadfast love never ceases and his mercies are new every morning, great is his faithfulness, and he is good to those who wait for him.

4.title: The Distress of Zion
4.context: The fourth lament contrasts Zion’s former glory with its present misery: gold has lost its luster, nobles starve and mothers cook their children, because of the sins of prophets and priests; it ends by declaring Zion’s punishment complete.

5.title: A Prayer for Restoration
5.context: The final chapter is the community’s prayer: it asks Yahweh to remember their disgrace, confesses their sin and pleads that he restore them as in days of old, unless he has utterly rejected them.

1.title: Ezekiel’s Vision by the River Kebar
1.context: In the fifth year of exile the priest Ezekiel, by the Kebar River in Babylon, sees a vision: four living creatures in a storm, wheels within wheels, and above them a throne bearing the likeness of the glory of Yahweh, at which he falls facedown.

2.title: Ezekiel’s Call
2.context: Yahweh tells “son of man” to stand up; the Spirit enters him and he is sent to the rebellious house of Israel, whether they listen or not; he eats a scroll written with lament, mourning and woe, and it tastes as sweet as honey.

3.title: A Watchman for Israel
3.context: After seven days Yahweh appoints Ezekiel a watchman for the house of Israel: if he warns the wicked and they do not turn, he saves himself; if he fails to warn, he is accountable for their blood.

3.title: Ezekiel Is Made Mute for a Time
3.context: The hand of Yahweh is on him in the plain, where the glory appears again; Ezekiel is told to shut himself in his house, and his tongue will cling to the roof of his mouth until Yahweh opens it.

4.title: A Sign of Jerusalem’s Siege
4.context: Ezekiel is told to draw Jerusalem on a clay brick and play out a siege, lying on his left side 390 days and on his right 40 days to bear the sin of Israel and Judah, and to eat rationed bread and drink rationed water.

5.title: The Razor of Judgment
5.context: Ezekiel takes a sharp sword as a razor and shaves his head and beard, dividing the hair into thirds: one burned, one struck with the sword, one scattered to the wind, showing the fate of Jerusalem, which has rebelled more than the nations around her.

6.title: Judgment against Idolatry
6.context: Ezekiel prophesies against the mountains of Israel: their high places and altars will be destroyed, the idols shattered, the slain fall among them; a remnant that escapes will remember Yahweh among the nations, and know that he is Yahweh.

7.title: The Hour of Doom
7.context: The end has come: Yahweh will judge Israel according to its ways without pity, and its silver and gold will not save it on the day of his wrath.

7.title: The Desolation of Israel
7.context: The trumpet is blown and all is ready, but no one goes to battle; sword outside, plague and famine inside, and survivors mourn like doves of the valleys, each for his own sin.

8.title: The Vision of Idolatry in the Temple
8.context: Ezekiel is carried in a vision to Jerusalem and sees an idol that provokes jealousy at the temple, elders worshiping creeping things in secret, women weeping for Tammuz and twenty-five men with their backs to the temple bowing to the sun.

9.title: Execution of the Idolaters
9.context: Yahweh calls out six executioners and a man in linen with a writing kit; the man marks the foreheads of those who grieve over the detestable things done in the city, and the others are told to strike down everyone else without mercy, starting at the sanctuary.

10.title: God’s Glory Exits the Temple
10.context: Ezekiel sees again the cherubim and wheels, and the man in linen takes burning coals from between the cherubim to scatter over the city; the glory of Yahweh rises from the cherub, moves to the threshold of the temple and stops at the east gate.

11.title: Evil in High Places
11.context: Twenty-five leaders give wicked counsel, saying the city is a pot and they are the meat; while Ezekiel prophesies against them, Pelatiah dies, and Ezekiel cries out asking whether Yahweh will destroy the whole remnant.

11.title: A Promise of Restoration
11.context: Yahweh says that though the exiles are scattered, he has been a sanctuary to them where they are; he will gather them back, remove their heart of stone, give them a heart of flesh, and they will be his people.

11.title: God’s Glory Leaves Jerusalem
11.context: The cherubim spread their wings with the wheels beside them, and the glory of the God of Israel is above them; the glory of Yahweh goes up from within the city and stops above the mountain east of it. The Spirit brings Ezekiel back to the exiles in Babylonia, and he tells them everything Yahweh has shown him.

12.title: Signs of the Coming Captivity
12.context: Yahweh tells Ezekiel to pack baggage for exile, carry it out in daylight, then dig through the wall at dusk and carry it out covering his face — a sign that the prince in Jerusalem and all the house of Israel will go into exile.

12.title: A Sign of Anxiety and Fear
12.context: Ezekiel is to eat his food trembling and drink his water shaking with anxiety, a sign that the people living in Jerusalem will eat in anxiety and drink in despair, because their land will be stripped of everything on account of their violence.

12.title: The Presumptuous Proverb
12.context: The people have a saying that days go by and visions come to nothing; Yahweh says the saying will end, for what he says will happen without delay.

13.title: Reproof of False Prophets
13.context: Ezekiel is to prophesy against Israel’s prophets who prophesy out of their own imagination: they have seen false visions and lying divinations, like jackals among ruins; they cry “Peace” when there is no peace, whitewashing a flimsy wall that a storm will bring down.

13.title: Reproof of False Prophetesses
13.context: Against the women who prophesy out of their own imagination: they sew magic charms on wrists and make veils to hunt people’s lives, profaning Yahweh among his people for handfuls of barley and scraps of bread; Yahweh will tear off their charms and rescue his people from their hands.

14.title: Idolatrous Elders Condemned
14.context: Some elders of Israel come to inquire of Yahweh, but they have set up idols in their hearts; Yahweh asks, “Should I let them inquire of me at all?” and calls the house of Israel to repent and turn from all their detestable practices; if a prophet is deceived, Yahweh will deal with both.

14.title: Four Dire Judgments
14.context: Yahweh declares that if a land sins against him, he may send famine, wild beasts, sword or plague, and even if Noah, Daniel and Job were in it, they would save only their own lives by their righteousness; a few survivors who escape will show Ezekiel how right his judgment on Jerusalem was.

15.title: Jerusalem the Useless Vine
15.context: Yahweh asks how the wood of a vine is better than the wood of a forest tree: it cannot be used for any craft, only burned; so he will treat the people of Jerusalem like the wood of the vine, giving them as fuel to the fire.

16.title: Jerusalem’s Unfaithfulness
16.context: Yahweh recounts Jerusalem’s history as a foundling: abandoned at birth, she was taken in by Yahweh, grew, was clothed and covered, and entered a covenant with him, but she trusted in her beauty and prostituted herself with every passer-by.

16.title: Jerusalem Like an Adulteress
16.context: Jerusalem builds mounds and lofty shrines on every street and spreads her legs for everyone; she lusts after Egypt, Assyria and Babylon, and even pays her lovers instead of being paid, and sacrifices to idols the sons and daughters she bore to Yahweh.

16.title: Judgment on Jerusalem
16.context: Because Jerusalem prostituted herself with the nations and gave her children to idols, Yahweh will hand her over to her lovers, strip her and judge her as an adulteress is judged.

16.title: Like Mother, Like Daughter
16.context: People will say of her, like mother, like daughter; she is more corrupt than her sisters Samaria and Sodom, and Sodom’s sin was pride, excess and failure to help the poor and needy.

16.title: Sodom and Samaria Will Be Restored
16.context: Yet Yahweh will restore the fortunes of Sodom and Samaria and her daughters, and also Jerusalem’s fortunes, so that she bears her disgrace and is a comfort to them; they will return to their former state.

16.title: The Covenant Remembered
16.context: Though Yahweh will punish her for despising her oath, he will remember his earlier covenant and establish an everlasting covenant with her, so that she knows he is Yahweh and is ashamed when he forgives her.

17.title: The Parable of Two Eagles and a Vine
17.context: A riddle and parable: a great eagle with powerful wings takes the very top of a cedar to a land of merchants, and plants a seed of the land beside abundant water where it grows into a low vine; but the vine turns its roots toward another great eagle, hoping for water.

17.title: The Parable Explained
17.context: The explanation: the first eagle is the king of Babylon who took Jehoiachin and installed Zedekiah under oath; Zedekiah rebelled and sought horses from Egypt, so he will die in Babylon, for he despised the oath and broke the covenant, “which was my oath and my covenant,” says Yahweh.

17.title: God's Promise for the Future
17.context: Yahweh himself will take a shoot from the very top of a cedar and plant it on a high mountain of Israel, where it will produce branches and fruit and become a splendid cedar; birds of every kind will nest in it, and all the trees will know that he brings low the tall tree and makes the low tree grow tall.

19.title: A Lament for the Princes of Israel
19.context: A lament for Israel’s princes: the lioness’s cubs are captured one after another and taken to Egypt and Babylon; the mother, like a vine, is uprooted and planted in the desert.

20.title: Israel’s Rebellion in Egypt
20.context: In the seventh year some elders come to inquire of Yahweh, and he refuses to be inquired of; Ezekiel recounts Israel’s rebellion from Egypt through the wilderness, how Yahweh gave them statutes and his Sabbaths as a sign, yet they rebelled and he held back his wrath for the sake of his name.

20.title: Judgment and Restoration
20.context: With a mighty hand Yahweh will bring his people out of the nations and judge them face to face in the “wilderness of the peoples,” purge the rebels and then accept them on his holy mountain.

20.title: A Prophecy against the South
20.context: Ezekiel is told to set his face toward the south and prophesy against the forest of the Negev: Yahweh will set fire to it, consuming every green tree and every dry tree, a fire that all will see is kindled by him and cannot be quenched; Ezekiel complains that they say of him, “Isn’t he just telling parables?”

21.title: God’s Sword of Judgment
21.context: Yahweh’s sword is sharpened and polished against Jerusalem and the land of Israel, cutting off righteous and wicked alike; Ezekiel is to groan and clap his hands as a sign of the coming disaster.

21.title: The Sword of the King of Babylon
21.context: At a fork in the road the king of Babylon divines and chooses to attack Jerusalem rather than Ammon; Yahweh declares that Israel’s wicked prince will lose his crown until the one to whom it rightfully belongs comes.

21.title: The Sword and the Ammonites
21.context: The sword will also come against the Ammonites who insulted Israel; they will be fuel for the fire and no longer remembered.

22.title: The Sins of Jerusalem
22.context: Jerusalem is a city of bloodshed, where parents are despised, foreigners oppressed, Sabbaths profaned and bribes taken; Yahweh will scatter them among the nations and melt them like dross in a furnace.

22.title: The Refining Furnace
22.context: The house of Israel has become dross to Yahweh, like the leftover when silver is smelted; so he will gather them into Jerusalem as one gathers metal into a furnace to melt it with fire, and he will melt them in his fury and anger, so they will know that Yahweh has poured out his wrath on them.

22.title: Israel’s Wicked Leaders
22.context: Prophets, priests, officials and people are all corrupt — prophets like roaring lions, priests who make no distinction between holy and common, officials like wolves; Yahweh looks for someone to stand in the gap but finds no one.

23.title: The Two Adulterous Sisters
23.context: Two sisters, daughters of one mother — Oholah (Samaria) and Oholibah (Jerusalem) — became prostitutes in Egypt in their youth, and belonged to Yahweh and bore him sons and daughters; Oholah lusted after Assyria and was handed over to her lovers, who stripped her and put her to the sword.

23.title: Oholibah to Be Plagued
23.context: Yahweh will stir up against Oholibah (Jerusalem) her former lovers, Babylon and others, and she will drink the same cup as her sister Samaria.

23.title: Judgment on Both Sisters
23.context: Yahweh tells Ezekiel to judge Oholah and Oholibah, who worshiped idols, sacrificed their children and defiled his sanctuary and Sabbaths, so they will receive the penalty of adulteresses and murderers.

24.title: The Parable of the Cooking Pot
24.context: On the day Babylon begins its siege of Jerusalem, Yahweh describes the city as a rusty pot whose meat is boiled away and whose corrosion cannot be removed except by burning.

24.title: Ezekiel’s Wife Dies
24.context: Yahweh tells Ezekiel that his beloved wife will die and that he must not mourn openly, as a sign that when the people lose their beloved temple and children, they too will be unable to mourn as usual.

25.title: A Prophecy against Ammon
25.context: A prophecy against the Ammonites: because they said “Aha!” over the sanctuary when it was desecrated, the land of Israel when it was laid waste and the people of Judah when they went into exile, Yahweh will give them to the people of the East as a possession, and they will know that he is Yahweh.

25.title: A Prophecy against Moab
25.context: A prophecy against Moab (and Seir): because they said Judah has become like all the other nations, Yahweh will expose Moab’s flank, her frontier towns, and give her to the people of the East along with the Ammonites.

25.title: A Prophecy against Edom
25.context: A prophecy against Edom: because Edom took revenge on Judah and incurred great guilt, Yahweh will stretch out his hand against Edom, cut off its people and animals, and lay it waste from Teman to Dedan; he will take vengeance on Edom by the hand of his people Israel.

25.title: A Prophecy against the Philistines
25.context: A prophecy against the Philistines: because they acted in vengeance and with malice in their hearts sought to destroy Judah in ancient enmity, Yahweh will stretch out his hand against them and cut off the Kerethites; he will carry out great vengeance on them, and they will know that he is Yahweh.

26.title: A Prophecy against Tyre
26.context: Because Tyre rejoiced at Jerusalem’s fall, Yahweh will bring many nations against it like waves; Nebuchadnezzar will tear down its walls, and it will become a bare rock for spreading nets.

27.title: A Lament for Tyre
27.context: A lament for Tyre pictures it as a magnificent merchant ship built of the finest materials and enriched by trade with many nations, which finally sinks in the heart of the sea while all the traders are appalled.

28.title: A Prophecy against the Ruler of Tyre
28.context: The ruler of Tyre is proud at heart and claims to sit on a god’s throne, wiser than Daniel; Yahweh says he is only a man and will die at the hands of foreigners.

28.title: A Lament for the King of Tyre
28.context: A lament for the king of Tyre uses images of Eden, precious stones and an anointed cherub to describe how he was blameless at first, then sinned through widespread trade and pride and was cast down and burned to ashes. Readers interpret these images in different ways.

28.title: A Prophecy against Sidon
28.context: Yahweh will display his glory against Sidon, sending plague and sword into its streets so that it knows he is Yahweh.

28.title: The Restoration of Israel
28.context: The nations will no longer be thorns to Israel; Yahweh will gather Israel back to the land he gave Jacob, and they will live there securely, building houses and planting vineyards.

29.title: A Prophecy against Pharaoh
29.context: Pharaoh is like a great monster in the Nile who boasts that he made the river; Yahweh will hook him and throw him into the desert, and Egypt will lie desolate for forty years and afterwards be a lowly kingdom.

29.title: Egypt the Reward of Nebuchadnezzar
29.context: Nebuchadnezzar’s long siege of Tyre brought his army no reward, so Yahweh gives him Egypt as wages for his troops.

30.title: A Lament for Egypt
30.context: The day of Yahweh is near, a time of doom for the nations; Egypt and its allies will fall by the sword, the Nile will dry up and Egypt’s cities will burn.

30.title: Pharaoh’s Power Broken
30.context: Yahweh has broken one of Pharaoh’s arms and will break the other, while strengthening the arms of Babylon’s king and putting a sword in his hand.

31.title: Egypt Will Fall like Assyria
31.context: Ezekiel tells Pharaoh a parable: Assyria was once like a towering cedar of Lebanon, envied by all the trees, yet it was cut down for its pride, and Egypt will fall the same way.

32.title: A Lament for Pharaoh King of Egypt
32.context: A lament for Pharaoh: he is like a monster in the seas, and Yahweh will catch him in a net, spread his flesh over the mountains and darken the lights of heaven over him.

32.title: Egypt Cast into the Pit
32.context: Egypt will go down to the realm of the dead to lie among the slain and uncircumcised nations — Assyria, Elam, Meshek, Tubal, Edom, Sidon and others.

33.title: Ezekiel the Watchman for Israel
33.context: Yahweh makes Ezekiel a watchman for Israel: if he fails to warn the wicked and they die, Yahweh will hold him responsible, but if he warns them and they do not turn, he has saved himself.

33.title: The Message of the Watchman
33.context: The people ask how they can live under the weight of their sins; Yahweh says he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked but wants them to turn and live, and each is judged by their present ways.

33.title: Word of Jerusalem’s Fall
33.context: In the twelfth year of the exile, on the fifth day of the tenth month, a man who has escaped from Jerusalem comes to Ezekiel and says, “The city has fallen!” The evening before he arrived, the hand of Yahweh had been on Ezekiel, and he opened his mouth before the man came, so Ezekiel is no longer mute.

33.title: The People's Sin
33.context: After Jerusalem’s fall, those left in the ruins argue that if Abraham, one man, inherited the land, surely they will; Yahweh says they still shed blood and worship idols and will not possess it.

33.title: The Result of the Prophet's Message
33.context: The people invite one another to come and hear Ezekiel, treating him like a singer of love songs with a beautiful voice, but they do not act on his words; when it all comes true, they will know a prophet was among them.

34.title: A Prophecy against Israel’s Shepherds
34.context: Yahweh condemns Israel’s shepherds for caring only for themselves, eating the fat and wearing the wool but not feeding, healing or searching for the flock, which is scattered and becomes food for wild animals.

34.title: The Good Shepherd
34.context: Yahweh himself will search for and shepherd his sheep, lead them to good pasture, seek the lost and bind up the injured; he will set over them one shepherd, his servant David, and make a covenant of peace with them.

35.title: A Prophecy against Mount Seir
35.context: On Mount Seir (Edom): because it harbored ancient hostility toward Israel, handed them to the sword in their calamity and sought to seize their land, Yahweh will make it desolate forever.

36.title: A Prophecy to the Mountains of Israel
36.context: Yahweh speaks to the mountains of Israel, which the nations mocked and seized; he will make them sprout branches and bear fruit again, and his people will return and multiply there.

36.title: A New Heart and a New Spirit
36.context: Yahweh says Israel profaned his name among the nations; for the sake of his holy name he will gather them, sprinkle clean water on them, give them a new heart and a new spirit, and move them to keep his decrees.

37.title: The Valley of Dry Bones
37.context: Yahweh brings Ezekiel to a valley full of dry bones and tells him to prophesy to them; the bones come together, flesh covers them, breath enters and they stand as a vast army; Yahweh says this is the whole house of Israel, whose graves he will open and in whom he will put his Spirit.

37.title: One Nation with One King
37.context: Ezekiel joins two sticks labeled Judah and Joseph into one, a sign that Yahweh will make Israel and Judah one nation under his servant David as king, with an everlasting covenant of peace and his dwelling among them.

38.title: A Prophecy against Gog
38.context: Yahweh foretells that in the latter days Gog of the land of Magog will lead a vast multinational army against Israel, living securely in unwalled villages, intending to plunder it.

38.title: God Punishes Gog
38.context: When Gog attacks Israel, Yahweh’s fury will flare up; he will shake the earth and send plague, torrential rain, hailstones and burning sulfur so that the nations know he is Yahweh.

39.title: The Slaughter of Gog’s Armies
39.context: Gog’s armies will fall on the mountains of Israel and become food for birds and beasts, and Israel will burn their weapons as fuel for seven years.

39.title: The Burial of Gog
39.context: Israel will spend seven months burying Gog’s hordes in a valley renamed Hamon Gog to cleanse the land, and Yahweh invites birds and beasts to his sacrificial feast.

39.title: Israel to Be Restored
39.context: The nations will see Yahweh’s judgment and know that Israel went into exile for its sin; Yahweh will have compassion on all Jacob’s house, pour out his Spirit on them and no longer hide his face.

40.title: The Man with a Measuring Rod
40.context: In the twenty-fifth year of exile Yahweh brings Ezekiel in visions to a high mountain in Israel, where a man with a linen cord and measuring rod tells him to report everything he sees to Israel.

40.title: The East Gate
40.context: The man measures the wall surrounding the temple area with his rod of six long cubits, then goes to the gate facing east and goes up its steps, measuring the threshold, the guardrooms, the portico and the dimensions of the gateway, giving the dimensions of the outer east gate.

40.title: The Outer Court
40.context: The man brings Ezekiel into the outer court, which has a pavement and thirty rooms around it.

40.title: The North Gate
40.context: The man measures the north gate of the outer court, whose rooms, portico, windows and carved palm trees match the east gate.

40.title: The South Gate
