40.context: He then measures the south gate, which has the same dimensions as the others, with seven steps leading up to it.

40.title: The Gates of the Inner Court
40.context: He takes Ezekiel through the south gate into the inner court and measures its gates, which match the outer gates and have eight steps.

40.title: The East Gate of the Inner Court
40.context: He measures the east gate of the inner court, which has the same dimensions as the other gates, with palm trees carved on its pillars.

40.title: The North Gate of the Inner Court
40.context: Then he brings Ezekiel to the north gate and measures it; it has the same measurements as the others, with its alcoves, projecting walls and portico, windows all around, fifty cubits long and twenty-five wide, with the portico facing the outer court, palm trees on its jambs and eight steps up.

40.title: Eight Tables for Sacrifices
40.context: By the inner gate are a room for washing burnt offerings and eight tables for slaughtering sacrifices, with four more of cut stone, along with rooms for the singers and for the priests who guard the temple and the altar.

40.title: The Inner Court
40.context: The inner court is square with the altar in front of the temple, and the temple portico has steps and two pillars.

41.title: Outside the Temple
41.context: Around the temple are side rooms on three levels, thirty on each level and growing wider as they go up; the temple stands on a raised base, with a large building on the west.

41.title: The Building on the West
41.context: The building facing the temple yard on the west side is seventy cubits wide, its wall five cubits thick all around and its length ninety cubits.

41.title: The Measurements of the Temple
41.context: The man measures the temple, a hundred cubits long; the yard and the building with its walls are also a hundred cubits long, and the front of the temple with the yard to the east a hundred cubits wide.

41.title: The Interior Structures
41.context: The temple’s inner walls are paneled with wood carved with cherubim and palm trees, each cherub having a human face and a lion’s face; before the sanctuary stands a wooden table.

41.title: The Doors
41.context: The outer sanctuary and the Most Holy Place each have double doors with folding leaves, also carved with cherubim and palm trees.

42.title: Chambers for the Priests
42.context: North and south of the temple are chambers where the priests eat the most holy offerings, store them and change out of their sacred garments; the man then measures the whole sacred area, five hundred on each side.

42.title: The Outer Measurements
42.context: When he finishes measuring the inside of the temple area, he brings Ezekiel out through the east gate and measures all around: with his measuring rod he measures the east side, the north side, the south side and the west side, each five hundred cubits, with a wall around it to separate the holy from the common.

43.title: The Glory of Yahweh Returns to the Temple
43.context: Ezekiel sees the glory of the God of Israel enter the temple through the east gate and fill it; Yahweh says this is the place of his throne and the soles of his feet, where he will live among the Israelites forever.

43.title: The Altar of Sacrifice
43.context: The altar is measured in cubits, with a base, stepped ledges and horns at its corners, and steps facing east.

43.title: Dedicating the Altar
43.context: Yahweh gives instructions to purify and dedicate the altar with sin and burnt offerings over seven days; from the eighth day the priests may offer sacrifices on it and he will accept them.

44.title: The East Gate Assigned to the Prince
44.context: The outer east gate must stay shut because the God of Israel has entered through it; only the prince may sit inside it to eat in Yahweh’s presence.

44.title: Reproof of the Levites
44.context: Yahweh rebukes Israel for letting uncircumcised foreigners into his sanctuary and defiling his temple; such people must no longer enter.

44.title: Levites Who May Not Serve as Priests
44.context: The Levites who followed Israel into idolatry must bear their guilt; they may guard the gates and slaughter sacrifices but may not serve as priests.

44.title: The Duties of the Priests
44.context: The descendants of Zadok, who faithfully kept the sanctuary when Israel strayed, may come near to minister to Yahweh; they will wear linen, teach the people the difference between holy and common, and have Yahweh as their inheritance.

45.title: Consecration of the Land
45.context: When the land is divided, a holy district is to be set apart for Yahweh, holding the sanctuary and land for the priests and Levites, with the city’s property beside it.

45.title: The Prince’s Portion
45.context: The prince’s land lies on both sides of the holy district and the city, so that Israel’s princes will no longer oppress the people but leave the rest of the land to the tribes.

45.title: Honest Scales
45.context: Yahweh tells Israel’s princes to stop violence and oppression, do justice and use honest scales and measures; the people are to bring offerings to the prince, who will provide the sacrifices for the festivals.

45.title: The Feasts
45.context: On the first day of the first month a sin offering cleanses the sanctuary; Passover is kept on the fourteenth day, and a seven-day feast begins on the fifteenth of the seventh month, with the prince providing offerings for himself and the people.

46.title: The Prince’s Offerings
46.context: The inner east gate is shut on the six working days and opened on Sabbaths and New Moons; the prince enters by its portico to offer sacrifices while the people worship at the entrance, and at festivals the people enter by one gate and leave by the opposite one.

46.title: The Daily Offerings
46.context: Every morning a year-old lamb without defect is to be offered as a burnt offering with a grain offering, as a lasting ordinance.

46.title: The Prince and the Land
46.context: If the prince gives an inheritance to one of his sons, it belongs to them permanently, but a gift to a servant returns to the prince in the year of freedom; the prince must not seize the people’s property.

46.title: The Courts for Boiling and Baking
46.context: The man shows Ezekiel where the priests boil the guilt and sin offerings and bake the grain offerings, and the corner courts of the outer court where the people’s sacrifices are cooked.

47.title: Waters from under the Temple
47.context: Water flows east from under the temple threshold, growing deeper until it becomes an uncrossable river; where it goes the Dead Sea becomes fresh and teems with fish, and trees on its banks bear fruit every month with leaves for healing — an image Revelation 22:1–2 takes up.

47.title: The Borders of the Land
47.context: Yahweh sets the borders of the land to be divided among the twelve tribes, with Joseph receiving two portions; foreigners who live among them and have children are also to receive an inheritance within the tribes.

48.title: The Portions for the Tribes
48.context: From north to south, seven tribes — Dan, Asher, Naphtali, Manasseh, Ephraim, Reuben and Judah — each receive a strip of land.

48.title: The Portions for the Priests and Levites
48.context: South of Judah lies the holy district for Yahweh, with the sanctuary at its center surrounded by land for the priests and Levites, and the city and its land beside it, with the prince’s land on either side.

48.title: The Portions for the Remaining Tribes
48.context: South of the holy district, five tribes — Benjamin, Simeon, Issachar, Zebulun and Gad — each receive a strip of land.

48.title: The City Gates and Dimensions
48.context: The city has three gates on each side, named after the twelve tribes of Israel; its circumference is eighteen thousand cubits, and from then on its name will be “Yahweh Is There.”

1.title: Daniel Removed to Babylon
1.context: In the third year of Jehoiakim, Nebuchadnezzar takes Jerusalem and brings young nobles to Babylon for training; Daniel and his three friends refuse the king’s food, and God gives them favor, learning and wisdom beyond all the others.

2.title: The Dream Revealed to Daniel
2.context: Nebuchadnezzar demands that his wise men tell him his dream and its meaning or be killed; Daniel asks for time and prays with his friends, and the mystery is revealed to him in a night vision, and he praises God: “Wisdom and power are his.”

2.title: Daniel Interprets the Dream
2.context: Daniel tells the king that only the God of heaven reveals such mysteries: the statue of gold, silver, bronze, iron and clay stands for successive kingdoms, and a stone cut without hands that smashes it and fills the earth stands for God’s everlasting kingdom.

2.title: Nebuchadnezzar Promotes Daniel
2.context: Nebuchadnezzar falls before Daniel and confesses that his God is the God of gods and Lord of kings; he makes Daniel ruler over the province of Babylon and, at his request, appoints his three friends.

3.title: Nebuchadnezzar’s Golden Statue
3.context: Nebuchadnezzar makes a gold image sixty cubits high and six wide and sets it up on the plain of Dura, ordering all officials and peoples to fall down and worship it when the music sounds, on pain of being thrown into a blazing furnace.

3.title: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego Accused
3.context: Some officials accuse Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego of refusing to worship the gold image; they tell the king that their God is able to rescue them from the furnace, but even if he does not, they will not serve his gods or bow to the image.

3.title: The Fiery Furnace
3.context: In fury the king heats the furnace seven times hotter and has the three men bound and thrown in; the soldiers who carry them are killed, yet the king sees four men walking unharmed in the fire, the fourth looking like a son of the gods.

3.title: Three Men Delivered and Promoted
3.context: The three come out of the fire without a hair singed or the smell of smoke; the king praises their God, forbids anyone to speak against him and promotes the three men.

4.title: Nebuchadnezzar Confesses God’s Kingdom
4.context: Nebuchadnezzar proclaims to the world the signs and wonders of the Most High: he dreamed of a great tree cut down to a stump while a holy watcher declared that all must know the Most High rules over human kingdoms.

4.title: Daniel Interprets the Second Dream
4.context: Daniel explains that the tree is the king, who will be driven from people to live with animals and eat grass for seven periods until he acknowledges that the Most High rules; he urges the king to break off his sins by doing right and showing mercy to the poor.

4.title: Nebuchadnezzar Restored
4.context: A year later, as the king boasts of building Babylon, the dream is fulfilled; when the time ends he looks up to heaven, his sanity returns, and he praises the eternal King, whose works are right and who can humble the proud.

5.title: Belshazzar’s Feast
5.context: King Belshazzar holds a great feast, drinking from the gold and silver vessels taken from the Jerusalem temple and praising idols; suddenly a hand writes on the wall, the king is terrified, and the queen recommends Daniel.

5.title: Daniel Interprets the Handwriting
5.context: Daniel reminds Belshazzar that he knew Nebuchadnezzar’s story yet exalted himself; the writing means numbered, weighed and divided — God has ended his reign, he is found wanting, and his kingdom goes to the Medes and Persians. That night Belshazzar is killed.

6.title: The Plot against Daniel
6.context: Darius makes Daniel a chief administrator, and jealous officials trick the king into banning prayer to anyone but him for thirty days; Daniel keeps praying three times a day toward Jerusalem and is thrown to the lions, but God sends his angel to shut their mouths, and the king decrees that all must revere Daniel’s God.

7.title: Daniel’s Vision of the Four Beasts
7.context: In Belshazzar’s first year Daniel dreams of four beasts rising from the sea: a lion with eagle’s wings, a bear, a four-headed leopard with wings, and a terrifying fourth beast with ten horns, among which a small horn speaks boastfully.

7.title: Daniel’s Vision of the Ancient of Days
7.context: Daniel sees thrones set up and the Ancient of Days seated in judgment, and the beast is slain; then one like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven and receives authority, glory and an everlasting kingdom that all peoples will serve. At his trial Jesus uses this image of himself (Matthew 26:64).

7.title: Daniel’s Visions Interpreted
7.context: One standing nearby explains that the four beasts are four kings; the fourth beast is a fourth kingdom whose small horn will oppress the holy people for a time, times and half a time, but after judgment the kingdom will be given to the holy people of the Most High forever.

8.title: Daniel’s Vision of the Ram and the Goat
8.context: In a vision Daniel sees a two-horned ram struck down by a goat with a single horn; when the goat’s great horn breaks, four horns replace it, and from one comes a small horn that takes away the daily sacrifice and tramples the sanctuary.

8.title: Gabriel Interprets Daniel’s Vision
8.context: Gabriel explains that the ram is the kings of Media and Persia and the goat is the king of Greece; later a fierce king will arise and cause great destruction but will be broken without human hand. The vision concerns the time of the end.

9.title: Daniel’s Prayer for His People
9.context: In Darius’s first year Daniel learns from Jeremiah that the seventy years of exile are nearly over, so he fasts, confesses and prays for his people: they have sinned, and he asks the Lord to hear, forgive and act for his own sake.

9.title: Gabriel’s Prophecy of the Seventy Weeks
9.context: While Daniel is still praying, Gabriel comes and tells him that seventy “sevens” are decreed to end sin and bring in everlasting righteousness, during which an anointed one will be cut off and the city and sanctuary destroyed. Readers calculate these periods in different ways.

10.title: Daniel’s Vision by the Tigris
10.context: In Cyrus’s third year, after fasting for three weeks, Daniel sees a man in linen by the Tigris and loses all strength; the man tells him that the prince of Persia resisted him for twenty-one days until Michael came to help.

11.title: Kings of the South and North
11.context: The messenger foretells long conflicts, marriage alliances and broken treaties between the “king of the South” and the “king of the North,” successors of the Greek empire.

11.title: The Wicked King of the North
11.context: A contemptible person will seize the kingdom by intrigue, desecrate the sanctuary, abolish the daily sacrifice and set up the abomination that causes desolation; but the people who know their God will stand firm, and the wise will instruct many.

12.title: The End Times
12.context: At that time Michael will arise, there will be distress such as never before, but everyone whose name is written in the book will be delivered; many who sleep in the dust will awake, and the wise will shine like stars. Daniel is told to seal the book and rest until the end.

1.title: Hosea’s Wife and Children
1.context: When Yahweh first speaks through Hosea, he tells him to take an adulterous wife, Gomer, and have children of unfaithfulness; their children are named Jezreel, Lo-Ruhamah (“not loved”) and Lo-Ammi (“not my people”), as a picture of Israel’s unfaithfulness to Yahweh.

1.title: Israel Will Be Restored
1.context: Yet the Israelites will be like the sand on the seashore, which cannot be measured or counted; where it was said, “You are not my people,” they will be called “children of the living God.” Judah and Israel will come together and appoint one leader. Paul quotes this in Romans 9:25–26.

2.title: Israel’s Adultery Rebuked
2.context: Like a wronged husband Yahweh brings charges against Israel: she chased her “lovers,” the Baals, thinking they gave her grain and wine, not knowing it was Yahweh who gave them, so he will take it all back and end her festivals.

2.title: God’s Mercy to Israel
2.context: Yahweh will lead her into the wilderness and speak tenderly to her, making the Valley of Achor a door of hope; she will call him “my husband,” he will betroth her forever in righteousness, love, compassion and faithfulness, and call “Not my people” “My people.”

3.title: Hosea Redeems His Wife
3.context: Yahweh tells Hosea to love his adulterous wife again, so he buys her back for silver and barley and has her live quietly for many days, a picture of Israel living many days without king or sacrifice before returning to seek Yahweh and David their king.

4.title: God’s Case against His People
4.context: Yahweh brings a charge against the land’s people, for there is no faithfulness, love or knowledge of God, only cursing, lying, murder, stealing and adultery, and even the animals waste away.

4.title: Condemning the Priests
4.context: The priests have rejected knowledge and forgotten God’s law, so the people are destroyed for lack of knowledge; the more priests, the more sin, and they feed on the people’s sin offerings, wanting them to sin more.

4.title: Condemning Idolatry
4.context: Wine and prostitution have taken away the people’s understanding; they consult wooden idols and sacrifice on hilltops, and Yahweh warns Judah not to follow Israel’s example.

5.title: Hosea Warns the Idolaters
5.context: Their deeds do not let them return to God, for a spirit of prostitution is in them; even when they bring flocks and herds to seek Yahweh, they will not find him, for he has withdrawn from them.

5.title: War between Judah and Israel
5.context: Yahweh says he will be like a moth and rot to Ephraim and Judah, then like a lion that tears them; Ephraim turns to Assyria for help but finds no cure, until they admit their guilt and seek his face.

6.title: The Unrepentance of Israel and Judah
6.context: The people say they will return to Yahweh, who will heal and revive them, but Yahweh says their love is like morning mist that quickly vanishes; he desires mercy, not sacrifice, words Jesus quotes in Matthew 9:13 and 12:7.

7.title: Ephraim’s Iniquity
7.context: Israel’s leaders delight in the people’s wickedness; like a heated oven their hearts burn with intrigue, they devour their kings one after another, and no one calls on Yahweh.

7.title: Israel and the Nations
7.context: Ephraim mixes with the nations like a flat cake not turned over; like a silly dove it calls to Egypt and then flies to Assyria, but does not return to Yahweh.

8.title: Israel Will Reap the Whirlwind
8.context: Israel has broken the covenant, set up kings without Yahweh and made a calf of silver and gold; they sow the wind and reap the whirlwind, forgetting their Maker while building palaces.

9.title: Israel’s Punishment
9.context: Israel should not rejoice like the nations, for they have been unfaithful to God; they will return to “Egypt” and eat unclean food in Assyria, for the days of punishment have come.

9.title: Israel's Sin and Its Consequences
9.context: Yahweh first found Israel like grapes in the desert, but they went to Baal Peor and became detestable; Ephraim’s glory will fly away like a bird and its children will be few.

9.title: Yahweh Judges Israel
9.context: All their wickedness is in Gilgal; there Yahweh hated them, and he will drive them from his house; Ephraim is blighted, its root withered, bearing no fruit.

9.title: A Prophet Speaks about Israel
9.context: The prophet says that because they have not obeyed God, he will reject them, and they will wander among the nations.

10.title: God Judges Israel
10.context: Israel has sinned since the days of Gibeah; Yahweh urges them to sow righteousness, reap unfailing love and break up their unplowed ground, for it is time to seek him, but they have plowed wickedness and reaped evil.

11.title: Out of Egypt I Called My Son
11.context: Yahweh recalls loving Israel as a child, calling his son out of Egypt, teaching him to walk and leading him with cords of kindness; the more he called, the more they turned away, yet he will not unleash his fierce anger, for he is God and not man. Matthew 2:15 quotes verse 1.

11.title: Israel and Judah Condemned
11.context: Ephraim surrounds Yahweh with lies and Israel with deceit; they make treaties with Assyria and send olive oil to Egypt.

12.title: Other Verdicts
12.context: Ephraim is like a merchant using dishonest scales, boasting of his wealth and thinking no one will find his sin; Yahweh reminds them that he brought them out of Egypt by a prophet and cared for them.

13.title: God’s Anger against Israel
13.context: Ephraim was once feared, but became guilty through Baal worship and died; Yahweh cared for them in the wilderness, yet once satisfied they forgot him, so he will pounce on them like a lion or leopard. Still, he speaks of ransoming them from the grave, which Paul echoes in 1 Corinthians 15:55.

14.title: A Call to Repentance
14.context: Hosea calls Israel to return to Yahweh with words of confession, asking him to take away their sins and admitting that Assyria cannot save them and their handmade idols are not gods.

14.title: A Promise of God’s Blessing
14.context: Yahweh promises to heal their waywardness and love them freely; he will be like the dew to Israel, and they will blossom like a lily and send down roots like the cedars of Lebanon.

14.title: Closing Words
14.context: Closing words: the wise will understand these things, for Yahweh’s ways are right; the righteous walk in them, but the rebellious stumble.

1.title: The Invasion of Locusts
1.context: The word of Yahweh comes to Joel son of Pethuel: locust swarms have stripped the land — vines, fig trees and grain — so that grain offering and drink offering are cut off from the temple; priests and farmers are called to lament, put on sackcloth, declare a fast and cry out to Yahweh, “for the day of Yahweh is near.”

2.title: The Army of Locusts
2.context: Blow the trumpet in Zion, for the day of Yahweh is near: a vast locust army sweeps in like soldiers, the land before them like Eden and behind them a desert, and Yahweh thunders at the head of his army.

2.title: Return with All Your Heart
2.context: Yahweh says that even now they should return to him with fasting, weeping and mourning, tearing their hearts rather than their garments, for he is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and abounding in love.

2.title: Restoration Promised
2.context: Yahweh becomes jealous for his land and takes pity on his people; he will drive away the northern army, send autumn and spring rains and repay the years the locusts ate, so they know he is among Israel.

2.title: I Will Pour Out My Spirit
2.context: Afterward Yahweh will pour out his Spirit on all people; sons and daughters will prophesy, old men dream dreams and young men see visions, and everyone who calls on Yahweh’s name will be saved. Peter quotes this at Pentecost (Acts 2:16–21).

3.title: Yahweh Judges the Nations
3.context: Yahweh will gather the nations in the Valley of Jehoshaphat and judge them for scattering his people, dividing his land and selling his children; he calls them to beat their plowshares into swords and come to judgment.

3.title: Blessings for God’s People
3.context: Yahweh roars from Zion and the heavens and earth shake, but he will be a refuge for his people; in that day the mountains will drip new wine, a fountain will flow from his house, and he will dwell in Zion.

1.title: Judgment on Israel’s Neighbors
1.context: Amos, a shepherd from Tekoa, prophesies in the days of Uzziah and Jeroboam II; he begins with Damascus and announces Yahweh’s judgment on Israel’s neighbors, each oracle opening “for three sins… even for four.”

1.title: Judgment on the Philistines
1.context: Gaza is judged for carrying off whole communities as captives and selling them to Edom; Yahweh will send fire on her walls and strongholds, and the rest of the Philistine cities will be cut off.

1.title: Judgment on Tyre
1.context: Tyre is judged for selling entire communities to Edom and breaking a treaty of brotherhood; fire will consume her fortresses.

1.title: Judgment on Edom
1.context: Edom is judged for pursuing his brother with the sword, stifling all compassion and nursing his anger forever; fire will consume Teman and the fortresses of Bozrah.

1.title: Judgment on Ammon
1.context: Ammon is judged for ripping open pregnant women in Gilead to extend her borders; fire will consume the walls of Rabbah, and her king and officials will go into exile together.

2.title: Judgment on Moab, Judah, and Israel
2.context: Moab is judged for burning the bones of Edom’s king to lime; fire will fall on Kerioth. By this point Amos’s hearers, listening to judgments on their enemies, are surely nodding.

2.title: Judgment on Judah
2.context: The circle closes in on Judah, judged for rejecting the law of Yahweh and not keeping his decrees, led astray by the false gods their ancestors followed; fire will consume the fortresses of Jerusalem.

2.title: God Judges Israel
2.context: Yahweh judges Israel: they sell the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals, trample the poor, and father and son use the same girl; Yahweh destroyed the Amorites for them, yet they made Nazirites drink wine and silenced the prophets.

3.title: Witnesses against Israel
3.context: Do two walk together unless they agree? The Lord Yahweh does nothing without revealing his plan to the prophets; when a lion roars, who is not afraid, and when Yahweh speaks, who can but prophesy?

3.title: The End of Samaria
3.context: Yahweh summons Ashdod and Egypt to witness the turmoil and oppression in Samaria; an enemy will overrun the land, and Israel will be rescued only like two legs or a piece of ear snatched from a lion’s mouth.

4.title: Israel's Failure
4.context: Yahweh mocks them for multiplying sacrifices at Bethel and Gilgal and boasting of freewill offerings; he sent famine, drought, blight and plague, yet they did not return to him, so they must prepare to meet their God.

5.title: A Lamentation against Israel
5.context: Amos laments over Israel and urges them to seek Yahweh and live rather than seek Bethel; they hate those who uphold justice in court, so Yahweh despises their feasts and wants justice to roll on like a river and righteousness like a never-failing stream.

6.title: Woe to Those at Ease in Zion
6.context: Woe to those at ease in Zion and secure on Mount Samaria: they lounge on ivory beds, feast on lambs, drink wine by the bowl and play music, but do not grieve over Joseph’s ruin, so they will be the first into exile.

7.title: The Locusts, Fire, and Plumb Line
7.context: In a vision Amos sees Yahweh preparing locusts to strip the land; he pleads for Jacob, and Yahweh relents.

7.title: The Vision of Fire
7.context: Amos then sees Yahweh calling for fire to consume the deep and the land; he pleads again, and Yahweh relents again.

7.title: The Vision of the Plumb Line
7.context: Amos sees the Lord standing by a wall with a plumb line in his hand; Yahweh says he is setting a plumb line among Israel and will spare them no longer: the high places will be ruined and the house of Jeroboam will fall by the sword.

7.title: Amaziah Accuses Amos
7.context: Amaziah the priest of Bethel reports Amos to the king and tells him to go back to Judah; Amos replies that he was a shepherd and tended sycamore figs, not a prophet, until Yahweh sent him, and he announces Amaziah’s fate.

8.title: The Basket of Summer Fruit
8.context: Amos sees a basket of summer fruit, and Yahweh uses a wordplay to say the “end” has come for Israel; palace songs will turn to wailing.

8.title: The End of Israel
8.context: Yahweh condemns merchants who trample the needy, eager for the Sabbath to end so they can sell grain with dishonest measures; in that day the sun will set at noon and there will be a famine — not of bread, but of hearing Yahweh’s words.

9.title: The Destruction of Israel
9.context: Amos sees the Lord standing by the altar and ordering the tops of the pillars struck so that the thresholds shake; wherever people flee — to the grave, heaven, Carmel or the sea floor — Yahweh will find them, and he will sift Israel as grain is sifted.

9.title: A Promise of Restoration
9.context: In that day Yahweh will restore David’s fallen shelter so Israel possesses the remnant of Edom and all the nations called by his name; the plowman will overtake the reaper, the exiles will return and never again be uprooted. James quotes this in Acts 15:16–17.

1.title: The Destruction of Edom
1.context: Yahweh will make Edom small among the nations; it lives in rocky heights and proudly thinks no one can bring it down, but Yahweh will bring it low and even its allies will betray it.

1.title: Why Edom Is Punished
1.context: Edom is punished for violence against its brother Jacob: on the day Jerusalem fell it stood aloof and gloated, looted the city and cut down fugitives at the crossroads.

1.title: The Deliverance of Israel
1.context: The day of Yahweh is near for all nations; as Edom has done, so it will be done to it, and the nations will drink Yahweh’s wrath until they are as if they had never been.

1.title: Israel's Victory
1.context: On Mount Zion there will be deliverance, and Jacob’s house will possess its inheritance, while Esau’s house is burned up; deliverers will go up on Mount Zion to rule the mountains of Esau, and the kingdom will be Yahweh’s.

1.title: Jonah Flees from Yahweh
1.context: Yahweh sends Jonah to Nineveh, but he boards a ship for Tarshish in the opposite direction; Yahweh sends a great storm, the sailors’ lots fall on Jonah, he has them throw him overboard, the sea grows calm, and Yahweh provides a great fish to swallow him.

2.title: Jonah’s Prayer
2.context: Jonah spends three days and nights in the fish and prays to Yahweh, saying he cried out from the depths and Yahweh answered, and confessing that salvation comes from Yahweh; then the fish spits him out on dry land. Jesus uses this as a sign of himself (Matthew 12:40).

3.title: The Ninevites Repent
3.context: Yahweh sends Jonah a second time, and he proclaims in Nineveh that the city will be overthrown in forty days; from king to commoner they believe God, fast in sackcloth and turn from evil, and God relents from the disaster.

4.title: Jonah’s Anger at Yahweh’s Compassion
4.context: Jonah is angry that God spared the city, saying he knew God was gracious and merciful; Yahweh teaches him with a plant that grows and then withers: if Jonah cares about a plant, should God not care about Nineveh, with its 120,000 people and many animals?

1.title: Judgment to Come
1.context: Yahweh comes from his holy temple in judgment and the mountains melt beneath him, because of the sins of Samaria and Jerusalem; Samaria will become a heap of rubble and its idols will be smashed.

1.title: Weeping and Mourning
1.context: Micah laments the disaster coming on Judah’s towns using a string of wordplays on their names, for calamity has reached the gate of Jerusalem; he howls like a jackal and moans like an owl.

2.title: Woe to Oppressors
2.context: Woe to those who plot evil on their beds and at dawn seize other people’s fields and houses; Yahweh is planning disaster against them, yet the people prefer prophets who promise wine and beer.

3.title: Rulers and Prophets Condemned
3.context: Micah condemns rulers who hate good and love evil and devour the people as if stripping flesh from bones, prophets who prophesy for money and priests who teach for a price; therefore Zion will be plowed like a field and Jerusalem become rubble, a warning recalled in Jeremiah 26:18.

4.title: The Mountain of the House of Yahweh
4.context: In the last days the mountain of Yahweh’s temple will be established and peoples will stream to it to learn his ways; he will judge between nations, they will beat their swords into plowshares and no longer train for war, and each will sit under their own vine (as in Isaiah 2:2–4).

4.title: The Restoration of Zion
4.context: Yahweh will gather the lame and the exiles and make them a strong nation, reigning over them on Mount Zion; though Zion now writhes like a woman in labor and must go to Babylon, Yahweh will rescue her there.

5.title: A Ruler from Bethlehem
5.context: Though Bethlehem Ephrathah is small among Judah’s clans, from it will come one to rule over Israel, whose origins are from of old, from ancient days; he will shepherd his flock in the strength of Yahweh and be their peace. Matthew 2:6 uses this to point to Jesus’ birth in Bethlehem.

5.title: The Remnant of Jacob
5.context: The remnant of Jacob among the nations will be like dew from Yahweh and like a lion among the forest animals; in that day Yahweh will remove their horses, chariots, sorcery and idols.

6.title: The Case against Israel
6.context: Yahweh calls the mountains to hear his case against Israel, asking what he has done to weary them and reminding them how he redeemed them from Egypt and what Balak planned and Balaam answered, and what happened from Shittim to Gilgal, so they will know his saving acts.

6.title: The Punishment of Israel
6.context: How should one come before Yahweh? Not with thousands of rams, rivers of oil or even a firstborn; he has shown what is good: to act justly, love mercy and walk humbly with God. Yet the people keep dishonest scales, so they will eat and not be satisfied.

7.title: Israel’s Great Misery
7.context: The prophet laments that the godly have vanished; everyone lies in wait to shed blood, rulers and judges demand bribes, and no friend or family member can be trusted. Jesus echoes these words in Matthew 10:35–36.

7.title: Israel’s Confession and Comfort
7.context: The prophet tells his enemy not to gloat, for though he has fallen he will rise, and though he sits in darkness Yahweh will be his light; he will bear Yahweh’s anger until Yahweh pleads his case.

7.title: God’s Compassion on Israel
7.context: The prophet asks Yahweh to shepherd his people as in days of old; who is a God like him, pardoning sin, not staying angry forever, delighting in mercy? He will again have compassion, hurl their sins into the depths of the sea and show the love he swore to Abraham.

1.title: The Burden against Nineveh
1.context: Yahweh is a jealous and avenging God who will not leave the guilty unpunished; he rides in the whirlwind and the mountains quake before him, yet he is good, a refuge in times of trouble, and he will make an end of Nineveh so that trouble does not rise again.

2.title: The Overthrow of Nineveh
2.context: The prophet pictures the attackers storming Nineveh: chariots race through the streets, the river gates burst open and the palace collapses; the city that plundered nations like a lion’s den is stripped bare, for Yahweh says he is against it.

1.title: Habakkuk’s First Complaint
1.context: Habakkuk asks Yahweh how long he must cry for help and why he tolerates violence and injustice while the law is paralyzed and justice never prevails.

1.title: Yahweh’s Answer
1.context: Yahweh answers that he is raising up the Chaldeans (Babylonians), a ruthless and impetuous nation with horses swifter than leopards, who sweep across the earth, mock kings and make their own strength their god. Paul cites verse 5 in Acts 13:41.

1.title: Habakkuk’s Second Complaint
1.context: Habakkuk asks again how Yahweh, whose eyes are too pure to look on evil, can let the wicked swallow up those more righteous than themselves, catching people like fish in a net.

2.title: Yahweh Answers Again
2.context: Habakkuk stands at his watchpost to wait for an answer; Yahweh tells him to write the vision plainly, for it awaits its appointed time and will surely come though it lingers; the proud are not upright, but the righteous will live by faith, which Paul cites in Romans 1:17 and Galatians 3:11.

2.title: Woe to the Chaldeans
2.context: Five woes announce the fate of the Chaldeans, who plunder nations, gain wealth unjustly, build cities with blood, make neighbors drunk and trust mute idols; all will be repaid, but Yahweh is in his holy temple, and all the earth should be silent before him.

3.title: Habakkuk’s Prayer
3.context: Habakkuk’s prayer recalls Yahweh’s mighty appearances of old and asks him to remember mercy in his wrath; it ends by saying that even if the fig tree does not bud and the stalls are empty, he will still rejoice in Yahweh and be joyful in God his Savior.

1.title: Zephaniah Prophesies Judgment on Judah
1.context: In Josiah’s day Zephaniah announces that Yahweh will sweep away everything from the earth, especially those in Judah who worship Baal, the stars and Molek; the great day of Yahweh is near, a day of wrath, distress and darkness when silver and gold cannot save.

2.title: A Call to Repentance
2.context: Zephaniah urges the shameless nation to gather before Yahweh’s anger arrives; the humble who obey him should seek righteousness and humility, and perhaps they will be sheltered on the day of his wrath.

2.title: Judgment on the Philistines
2.context: Yahweh will judge the surrounding nations — Philistia, Moab, Ammon, Cush and Assyria’s Nineveh — for their pride and insults against his people, and Judah’s remnant will possess the Philistine coast and the lands of Moab and Ammon.

3.title: Judgment on Jerusalem
3.context: Jerusalem does not obey, accept correction or trust Yahweh; its officials are roaring lions, its prophets treacherous and its priests profane the sanctuary; but Yahweh will purify the lips of the peoples to call on him and leave a humble, lowly remnant who do no wrong.

3.title: Israel’s Restoration
3.context: Zion is told to sing, for Yahweh has taken away her punishment and reigns among her; the Mighty One who saves will rejoice over her with gladness, quiet her with his love and delight in her with singing, and he will gather the scattered and give them praise throughout the earth.

1.title: A Call to Rebuild the Temple
1.context: The returned exiles say it is not yet time to rebuild the temple while they live in paneled houses; through Haggai Yahweh says their harvests are poor and their wages vanish like money in a bag with holes because his house lies in ruins, so they must bring timber and build.

1.title: The People Obey
1.context: Governor Zerubbabel, high priest Joshua and the whole remnant obey Yahweh and fear him; Yahweh says he is with them and stirs their spirits, and they begin work on the temple.

2.title: The Coming Glory of God’s House
2.context: Older people think the new temple is nothing compared with Solomon’s; Yahweh encourages them to be strong and work, for he is with them; he will shake heaven, earth and the nations, their treasures will come, and the glory of this house will be greater than the former.

2.title: Blessings for a Defiled People
2.context: Haggai asks the priests whether holy meat makes other food holy by touch; they say no, but an unclean person does make food unclean; likewise, the people’s uncleanness has defiled what they offer.

2.title: Yahweh Promises Blessing
2.context: Yahweh tells the people to recall how meager their harvests were before the temple foundation was laid; from this day on he will bless them.

2.title: Zerubbabel Yahweh’s Signet Ring
2.context: Yahweh will shake the heavens and earth and overthrow the thrones of kingdoms, and on that day he will make Zerubbabel like his signet ring, for he has chosen him.

1.title: A Call to Repentance
1.context: In the eighth month of Darius’s second year, Yahweh calls the people through Zechariah not to be like their ancestors: “Return to me, and I will return to you.”

1.title: The Vision of the Horses
1.context: The first night vision: a man on a red horse among myrtle trees reports that the earth is at rest; the angel pleads for Jerusalem, and Yahweh promises to return with mercy and rebuild his house.

1.title: The Vision of the Horns and the Craftsmen
1.context: The second vision: four horns, the nations that scattered Judah, and four craftsmen who come to throw them down.

2.title: The Vision of the Measuring Line
2.context: The third vision: a man with a measuring line goes to measure Jerusalem, but it will be a city without walls because of its many people, and Yahweh will be a wall of fire around it and its glory within.

2.title: The Redemption of Zion
2.context: Yahweh calls the exiles to flee from the land of the north; Zion is to sing for joy, for he is coming to dwell among them, and many nations will join themselves to him in that day.

3.title: The Vision of Joshua the High Priest
3.context: The fourth vision: Joshua the high priest stands before the angel of Yahweh in filthy clothes, with the Accuser beside him; Yahweh rebukes the Accuser, Joshua is given clean garments, and Yahweh promises to bring his servant, the Branch.

4.title: The Vision of the Lampstand and Olive Trees
4.context: Zechariah sees a solid gold lampstand with two olive trees beside it; the angel explains that Zerubbabel will build the temple not by might or power but by Yahweh’s Spirit, and the hands that laid the foundation will finish it.

4.title: God's Promise to Zerubbabel
4.context: Zerubbabel’s hands laid the temple’s foundation and will complete it; no one should despise the day of small things. The two olive trees are the two anointed ones who serve the Lord of all the earth.

5.title: The Vision of the Flying Scroll
5.context: The sixth vision: a flying scroll twenty cubits long and ten wide, a curse going out over the land against thieves and those who swear falsely.

5.title: The Vision of the Woman in a Basket
5.context: The seventh vision: a woman sitting in a measuring basket, named Wickedness, carried off by two winged women to Babylonia.

6.title: The Vision of the Four Chariots
6.context: The eighth vision: four chariots come out from between two bronze mountains and go out to the four winds; those going north give Yahweh’s Spirit rest there.

6.title: The Crown and the Temple
6.context: Yahweh tells Zechariah to make crowns from silver and gold brought by exiles and set one on Joshua the high priest, announcing that the man called the Branch will build the temple, rule on his throne and be a priest, with harmony between the two.

7.title: A Call to Justice and Mercy
7.context: Men from Bethel ask whether they should keep mourning and fasting in the fifth month as they have done for years; Yahweh asks whether those fasts were really for him.

7.title: Exile Was the Result of Disobedience
7.context: What Yahweh wants is true justice, mercy and compassion to one another, and no oppression of widows, orphans, foreigners or the poor; their ancestors refused to listen, so he scattered them among the nations.

8.title: The Restoration of Jerusalem
8.context: Yahweh is very jealous for Zion and will return to dwell in Jerusalem; old people will sit in the streets and children play there, the exiles will come back, fasts will become joyful festivals, and many peoples will come to seek him.

9.title: The Burden against Israel’s Enemies
9.context: An oracle: Yahweh’s word is against Hadrak, Damascus, Tyre, Sidon and the Philistine cities; he will judge Israel’s neighbors and guard his house.

9.title: Zion’s Coming King
9.context: Zion is to rejoice greatly, for her king comes, righteous and bringing salvation, humble and riding on a donkey’s colt; he will remove chariots and warhorses and proclaim peace to the nations. Jesus fulfills this when he rides into Jerusalem (Matthew 21:4–5; John 12:14–15).

9.title: Yahweh Will Save His People
9.context: Because of the blood of his covenant with them, Yahweh will free the prisoners; he will bend Judah as his bow and fill it with Ephraim, shield them and save them like a flock.

10.title: Judah and Israel Will Be Restored
10.context: Ask Yahweh for rain in springtime, not the idols and diviners; Yahweh will strengthen Judah, save the house of Joseph and bring them back from Egypt and Assyria.

11.title: The Doomed Flock
11.context: The cedars of Lebanon fall and the shepherds wail; Yahweh tells Zechariah to shepherd the flock marked for slaughter, whose buyers and sellers have no pity.

11.title: The Two Shepherds
11.context: Zechariah shepherds with two staffs, Favor and Union, then breaks them; his wages, thirty pieces of silver, he throws to the potter at Yahweh’s command. Matthew 27:9–10 refers to this in describing Judas’ silver.

12.title: The Coming Deliverance of Jerusalem
12.context: Yahweh will make Jerusalem a cup that sends the nations reeling and an immovable rock; he will pour on the house of David a spirit of grace and supplication, and they will look on the one they have pierced and mourn for him. John 19:37 applies this to Jesus.

13.title: The Shepherd Struck, the Sheep Scattered
13.context: Yahweh calls the sword to strike his shepherd so the sheep scatter; two-thirds of the land will be cut off and one-third refined by fire, they will call on his name and he will say, “They are my people.” Jesus quotes the words about the shepherd before his arrest (Matthew 26:31).

14.title: The Destroyers of Jerusalem Destroyed
14.context: When the day of Yahweh comes and the nations besiege Jerusalem, Yahweh will go out to fight them; his feet will stand on the Mount of Olives and it will split in two; living water will flow from Jerusalem, Yahweh will be king over the whole earth, and the nations will come up year by year to worship him.

1.title: Yahweh’s Love for Israel
1.context: Yahweh says through Malachi, “I have loved you,” and when they ask how, he points to the contrast between Jacob and Esau; Paul quotes this in Romans 9:13.

1.title: The Polluted Offerings
1.context: The priests despise Yahweh’s name by offering blind, lame and sick animals; he wishes someone would shut the temple doors, for his name will be great among the nations.

2.title: Judah’s Unfaithfulness
2.context: Do we not all have one Father and one God who created us? Why then are we faithless to one another? Judah has married women who worship foreign gods and broken faith with the wives of their youth; Yahweh says he hates divorce and calls them to guard their hearts and not be unfaithful.

2.title: The Day of Judgment Is Near
2.context: The people say Yahweh delights in evildoers; he answers that he will send his messenger to prepare the way before him, and the Lord they seek will suddenly come to his temple — who can endure the day of his coming? He will be like a refiner’s fire. The Gospels apply the messenger to John the Baptist (Matthew 11:10).

3.title: Robbing God
3.context: Yahweh says he does not change, so Jacob’s descendants are not destroyed; the people rob him in tithes and offerings, but if they bring the whole tithe into the storehouse, he will open the windows of heaven and pour out blessing.

3.title: The Book of Remembrance
3.context: Some say serving God is futile, but those who fear Yahweh talk together, and he listens; a scroll of remembrance is written before him concerning those who honor his name, and they will be his treasured possession.

4.title: The Day of Yahweh
4.context: The day is coming that burns like a furnace, consuming the arrogant like stubble, but for those who fear Yahweh’s name the sun of righteousness will rise with healing; Yahweh will send Elijah to turn parents’ hearts to their children. Jesus says John the Baptist is that Elijah (Matthew 11:14).

1.title: The Genealogy of Jesus
1.context: Matthew opens with the genealogy of Jesus the Messiah, descendant of Abraham and of David, in three sets of fourteen generations.

1.title: The Birth of Jesus
1.context: Before Mary and Joseph come together she is found to be with child by the Holy Spirit. An angel tells Joseph in a dream to name the child Jesus, because he will save his people from their sins.

2.title: The Pilgrimage of the Magi
2.context: Magi from the east, having seen his star, come to Jerusalem looking for the one born king of the Jews. King Herod is troubled, and all Jerusalem with him.

2.title: The Flight to Egypt
2.context: An angel warns Joseph in a dream, and he takes the child and his mother to Egypt until Herod dies. This fulfils “Out of Egypt I called my son” (Hos 11:1).

2.title: Weeping and Great Mourning
2.context: Furious, Herod has all the boys in Bethlehem and its vicinity two years old and under killed, fulfilling Jeremiah’s word about Rachel weeping for her children (Jer 31:15).

2.title: The Return to Nazareth
2.context: After Herod’s death an angel again speaks to Joseph in a dream; he brings the child and his mother back to the land of Israel and settles in Nazareth in Galilee.

3.title: The Mission of John the Baptist
3.context: John the Baptist preaches in the Judean wilderness, calling people to repent because the kingdom of heaven is near; he is the voice in the wilderness Isaiah spoke of, rebukes the Pharisees and Sadducees who come to him, and says the one coming after him will baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire.

3.title: The Baptism of Jesus
3.context: Jesus comes from Galilee to be baptized by John, who hesitates, but Jesus says it is fitting to fulfill all righteousness; as he comes up from the water, the Spirit of God descends on him like a dove and a voice from heaven calls him the beloved Son with whom God is pleased.

4.title: The Temptation of Jesus
4.context: Led by the Spirit into the wilderness, Jesus fasts forty days and nights and is tempted by the devil; each time he answers with “It is written.”

4.title: Jesus Begins His Ministry
4.context: When John is put in prison Jesus returns to Galilee and settles in Capernaum. He begins to preach, “The kingdom of heaven is near,” fulfilling Isaiah (Isa 9:1–2).

4.title: The First Disciples
4.context: By the Sea of Galilee Jesus calls Peter and Andrew, then James and John; they leave their nets and their boat and follow him.

4.title: Jesus Heals the Multitudes
4.context: Jesus goes throughout Galilee, teaching in the synagogues, proclaiming the good news of the kingdom and healing every disease and sickness among the people.

5.title: The Sermon on the Mount
5.context: Seeing the crowds, Jesus goes up on a mountainside and sits down; his disciples come to him and he begins to teach them (Matt 5–7).

5.title: The Beatitudes
5.context: Jesus pronounces eight kinds of people blessed: the poor in spirit, those who mourn, the meek, those who hunger for righteousness, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers, and the persecuted for righteousness.

5.title: Salt and Light
5.context: Jesus tells his disciples they are the salt of the earth and the light of the world; let people see their good deeds and glorify their Father in heaven.

5.title: The Fulfillment of the Law
5.context: Jesus says he has not come to abolish the Law or the Prophets but to fulfil them; not the smallest letter or stroke will disappear from the Law.

5.title: Anger and Reconciliation
5.context: Jesus takes “You shall not murder” deeper: anyone angry with a brother is subject to judgment; first be reconciled to your brother, then come and offer your gift.

5.title: Adultery
5.context: Jesus says anyone who looks at a woman lustfully has already committed adultery with her in his heart; it is better to lose one part of the body than for the whole body to be thrown into hell.

5.title: Divorce
5.context: Jesus teaches that anyone who divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, makes her an adulteress, and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery.

5.title: Oaths and Vows
5.context: Jesus says not to swear at all; let your “Yes” be yes and your “No” be no, for anything beyond this comes from the evil one.

5.title: Love Your Enemies
5.context: Jesus says not to resist with an eye for an eye: if someone strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other also. Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you.

5.title: On Loving Your Enemies
5.context: Jesus says to love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, so that you may be children of your Father in heaven, who makes his sun rise on the evil and the good and sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous.

6.title: Giving to the Needy
6.context: The Sermon on the Mount continues: give to the needy in secret, not to be seen by others, and your Father who sees in secret will reward you.

6.title: The Lord’s Prayer
6.context: Jesus teaches not to pray like hypocrites who want to be seen, but to pray to the Father in secret without empty repetition; he teaches the disciples to pray that the Father’s name be holy and his kingdom come, for daily bread and forgiveness, and says those who forgive others will be forgiven.

6.title: Proper Fasting
6.context: When you fast, do not look somber like the hypocrites; wash your face and anoint your head, so that only your Father in secret sees it.

6.title: Treasures in Heaven
6.context: Do not store up treasures on earth, where moth, rust and thieves destroy, but store them in heaven, for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.

6.title: The Lamp of the Body
6.context: The eye is the lamp of the body: a clear eye fills the whole body with light, a bad eye fills it with darkness.

6.title: On God and Money
6.context: No one can serve two masters; you cannot serve both God and money.

6.title: Do Not Worry
6.context: Jesus tells his disciples not to worry about food and clothing: the Father feeds the birds and clothes the lilies; seek first his kingdom and his righteousness and all these things will be given as well, for tomorrow will take care of itself.

7.title: Judging Others
7.context: Do not judge, or you too will be judged; first take the plank out of your own eye before removing the speck from your brother’s; do not give what is holy to dogs.

7.title: Ask, Seek, Knock
7.context: Ask, seek and knock, and it will be given; how much more will your Father in heaven give good gifts to those who ask him. So in everything, do to others what you would have them do to you.

7.title: The Narrow Gate
7.context: Enter through the narrow gate: wide is the road to destruction and many take it, but narrow is the road that leads to life, and few find it.

7.title: A Tree and Its Fruit
7.context: Watch out for false prophets in sheep’s clothing who inwardly are ferocious wolves; you will recognize them by their fruit.

7.title: I Never Knew You
7.context: Not everyone who says “Lord, Lord” will enter the kingdom of heaven, but only the one who does the will of the Father in heaven.

7.title: The House on the Rock
7.context: Whoever hears these words and does them is like a wise man who built his house on the rock; whoever does not is like a fool who built on sand. The crowds are amazed, because he teaches as one who has authority.

8.title: The Leper’s Prayer
8.context: After Jesus comes down the mountain, a man with leprosy kneels and says Jesus can make him clean if he is willing; Jesus touches him, says he is willing, heals him and tells him to show himself to the priest and offer the gift Moses commanded.

8.title: The Faith of the Centurion
8.context: A Roman centurion in Capernaum asks Jesus to heal his servant and says, “Just say the word”; Jesus marvels that he has not found such faith in Israel, and the servant is healed that hour.

8.title: Jesus Heals at Peter’s House
8.context: At Peter’s house Jesus touches the hand of Peter’s feverish mother-in-law, and she recovers and serves him; that evening he drives out many demons and heals all the sick, fulfilling Isaiah’s words that he took up our infirmities and carried our diseases.

8.title: The Cost of Discipleship
8.context: A scribe offers to follow Jesus wherever he goes, and Jesus says foxes have holes and birds have nests but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head; to another disciple who wants first to bury his father, he says to let the dead bury their own dead and follow him.

8.title: Jesus Calms the Storm
8.context: Jesus is asleep in a boat when a fierce storm arises; the disciples wake him begging for help, he rebukes their little faith and then the wind and waves, and there is a great calm; they marvel at what kind of man this is, whom even wind and sea obey.

8.title: The Demons and the Pigs
8.context: In the region of the Gadarenes two demon-possessed men meet Jesus; the demons beg to be sent into a herd of pigs, which rush down the bank into the lake and drown, and the townspeople plead with Jesus to leave.

9.title: Jesus Heals a Paralytic
9.context: Some men bring a paralyzed man, and seeing their faith Jesus says, “Your sins are forgiven”; to the scribes who think he is blaspheming, he shows that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins by telling the man to get up and go home. The crowds praise God, “who had given such authority to man.”

9.title: Jesus Calls Matthew
9.context: Jesus sees Matthew the tax collector at his booth and calls him, and Matthew follows; when Jesus eats with many tax collectors and sinners and the Pharisees object, he says the healthy do not need a doctor, and he came to call not the righteous but sinners.

9.title: Questions about Fasting
9.context: John’s disciples ask why Jesus’ disciples do not fast; he answers with images of the bridegroom, new patches on old garments and new wine in old wineskins.

9.title: The Healing Touch of Jesus
9.context: A synagogue leader begs Jesus to raise his daughter who has just died; on the way a woman who has bled for twelve years touches the edge of his cloak and is healed; at the house Jesus takes the girl by the hand and she gets up.

9.title: Jesus Heals the Blind and Mute
9.context: Two blind men follow Jesus calling him Son of David; he asks whether they believe he can heal them, they say yes, and when he touches their eyes they see; then he drives a demon out of a mute man, who begins to speak.

9.title: Jesus Heals a Mute Man
9.context: A mute, demon-possessed man is brought to Jesus; when the demon is driven out he speaks, and the crowd is amazed, but the Pharisees say Jesus drives out demons by the prince of demons.

9.title: The Lord of the Harvest
9.context: Jesus travels through all the towns and villages, teaching, proclaiming the good news of the kingdom and healing; seeing the crowds harassed and helpless like sheep without a shepherd, he has compassion and tells his disciples to ask the Lord of the harvest to send out workers.

10.title: The Twelve Apostles
10.context: Jesus calls his twelve disciples and gives them authority to drive out impure spirits and heal every disease; the names of the twelve apostles are listed.

10.title: The Ministry of the Twelve
10.context: Jesus sends out the twelve, first to the lost sheep of Israel, to proclaim that the kingdom of heaven has come near and to heal; “Freely you have received; freely give,” taking no money for the journey.

10.title: Sheep among Wolves
10.context: Jesus sends them like sheep among wolves, to be shrewd as snakes and innocent as doves; they will be handed over to councils and brought before governors and kings, but they should not worry what to say, for it will be the Spirit of their Father speaking through them.

10.title: Fear God Alone
10.context: Do not be afraid of those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear the one who can destroy both soul and body in hell. Not one sparrow falls without the Father’s knowledge; you are worth more than many sparrows.

10.title: Confessing Christ
10.context: Whoever acknowledges Jesus before others, he will acknowledge before his Father in heaven; whoever disowns him, he will disown.

10.title: Not Peace but a Sword
10.context: Jesus says he has not come to bring peace but a sword, setting family members against one another; anyone who loves parents or children more than him, or does not take up the cross and follow him, is not worthy of him; whoever loses their life for his sake will find it.

10.title: The Reward of Service
10.context: Whoever welcomes the disciples welcomes Jesus, and whoever welcomes him welcomes the one who sent him; even a cup of cold water given to one of these little ones will not lose its reward.

11.title: John’s Inquiry
11.context: John in prison sends to ask, “Are you the one who is to come?” Jesus points to the blind seeing, the lame walking, the dead raised and the good news proclaimed to the poor, and calls John more than a prophet, the Elijah who was to come.

11.title: Woe to the Unrepentant
11.context: Jesus denounces Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum, where most of his miracles were performed, because they did not repent; Tyre, Sidon and Sodom would have repented long ago.

11.title: Rest for the Weary
11.context: Jesus thanks the Father for hiding these things from the wise and revealing them to little children; he says all things have been committed to him by the Father and invites all who are weary and burdened to come to him, take his yoke and learn from him, for he is gentle and humble in heart, and they will find rest.

12.title: The Lord of the Sabbath
12.context: When the disciples pick grain on the Sabbath, the Pharisees object; Jesus cites David eating the consecrated bread and the priests working in the temple, quotes “I desire mercy, not sacrifice,” and declares that the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.

12.title: Jesus Heals on the Sabbath
12.context: In the synagogue Jesus heals a man with a shriveled hand, saying a person is worth more than a sheep and it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath; the Pharisees plot how to kill him.

12.title: God’s Chosen Servant
12.context: Aware that the Pharisees are plotting against him, Jesus withdraws, heals those who follow and tells them not to publicize it, fulfilling Isaiah’s words about God’s chosen servant who will not quarrel or shout, will not break a bruised reed, and in whose name the nations will hope.

12.title: A House Divided
12.context: Jesus heals a demon-possessed man who is blind and mute, and the Pharisees claim he drives out demons by the prince of demons; Jesus says a kingdom divided against itself cannot stand, and if he drives out demons by the Spirit of God, God’s kingdom has come; blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven.

12.title: Good and Bad Fruit
12.context: A tree is recognized by its fruit; the mouth speaks what the heart is full of, and on the day of judgment people will give account for every empty word they have spoken.

12.title: The Sign of Jonah
12.context: Some ask for a sign; Jesus says none will be given except the sign of Jonah: as Jonah was three days and nights in the fish, so the Son of Man will be three days and nights in the heart of the earth; the people of Nineveh and the Queen of the South will condemn this generation.

12.title: An Unclean Spirit Returns
12.context: When an impure spirit leaves a person and finds the house empty, it returns with seven spirits more wicked than itself, and the final condition is worse than the first; so it will be with this wicked generation.

12.title: Jesus’ Mother and Brothers
12.context: Jesus’ mother and brothers stand outside wanting to speak with him; pointing to his disciples, he says that whoever does the will of his Father in heaven is his brother, sister and mother.

13.title: The Parable of the Sower
13.context: From a boat by the lake Jesus tells the crowd the parable of the sower: seed falls on the path, on rocky ground, among thorns, and on good soil that yields a crop a hundred, sixty or thirty times.

13.title: The Purpose of Jesus’ Parables
13.context: The disciples ask why he speaks in parables; he says the secrets of the kingdom are given to them but not to others, fulfilling Isaiah’s prophecy of those who see but do not perceive.

13.title: The Parable of the Sower Explained
13.context: Jesus explains the sower: the seed is the message of the kingdom, and the four soils are four kinds of hearers, the good soil being the one who hears the word, understands it and bears fruit.

13.title: The Parable of the Weeds
13.context: The kingdom is like a man who sows good seed, but an enemy sows weeds among the wheat; at harvest the weeds are gathered and burned, and the wheat brought into the barn.

13.title: The Parable of the Mustard Seed
13.context: The kingdom is like a mustard seed, the smallest of seeds, which grows into a tree where birds nest; and like yeast mixed into a large amount of flour until it works through all the dough.

13.title: I Will Open My Mouth in Parables
13.context: Jesus speaks to the crowds in parables and says nothing to them without a parable, fulfilling the psalm: he will open his mouth in parables and utter things hidden since the creation of the world.

13.title: The Parable of the Weeds Explained
13.context: Jesus explains the weeds to his disciples: the sower is the Son of Man, the field is the world, the good seed the people of the kingdom, the weeds the people of the evil one, and the harvest the end of the age.

13.title: The Parables of the Treasure and the Pearl
13.context: The kingdom is like treasure hidden in a field, for which a man sells everything to buy the field; like a merchant who sells all he has to buy one pearl of great value; and like a net that catches all kinds of fish, to be sorted at the end of the age.

13.title: Things New and Old
13.context: Jesus asks if they have understood all this, and they say yes; every teacher of the law who has become a disciple in the kingdom is like a homeowner who brings out of his storeroom new treasures as well as old.

13.title: The Rejection at Nazareth
13.context: Jesus teaches in his hometown synagogue, and they are amazed yet take offense: “Isn’t this the carpenter’s son?” He says a prophet is not without honor except in his own town, and he does not do many miracles there because of their lack of faith.

14.title: The Beheading of John
14.context: Herod the tetrarch hears about Jesus and thinks John the Baptist has risen from the dead; the passage recalls how Herod had imprisoned John over Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife, and at his birthday feast Herodias’s daughter danced and asked for John’s head on a platter.

14.title: The Feeding of the Five Thousand
14.context: Jesus withdraws to a solitary place, and the crowds follow; in the evening he takes five loaves and two fish, looks up to heaven, gives thanks, breaks them and the disciples distribute them; all eat and are satisfied, twelve basketfuls are left over, and about five thousand men besides women and children are fed.

14.title: Jesus Walks on Water
14.context: At night Jesus walks on the sea toward the disciples’ boat and tells them not to fear; Peter walks on the water too but sinks when he sees the wind, and Jesus catches him and rebukes his little faith. Those in the boat worship him as the Son of God.

14.title: Jesus Heals at Gennesaret
14.context: At Gennesaret the people recognize Jesus and bring all their sick to him, begging to touch even the edge of his cloak, and all who touch it are healed.

15.title: The Tradition of the Elders
15.context: The Pharisees ask why the disciples break the elders’ tradition about washing hands before eating; Jesus asks why they nullify God’s command for their tradition, such as dedicating money to avoid honoring parents, and says it is not what goes into the mouth that defiles a person but what comes out of it.

15.title: The Faith of the Canaanite Woman
15.context: A Canaanite woman begs Jesus to heal her demon-possessed daughter; at first he does not answer and says he was sent only to the lost sheep of Israel, but when she replies that even dogs eat the crumbs from their masters’ table, he praises her great faith and her daughter is healed.

15.title: Jesus Heals Many
15.context: Jesus goes along the Sea of Galilee, sits on a mountainside, and great crowds bring the lame, blind, crippled and mute; he heals them, and the people praise the God of Israel.

15.title: Jesus Feeds the Four Thousand
15.context: Jesus has compassion on the crowd who have been with him three days without food; he takes seven loaves and a few small fish, gives thanks and breaks them, and the disciples distribute them; four thousand men besides women and children eat and are satisfied, with seven basketfuls left over.

16.title: The Demand for a Sign
16.context: Pharisees and Sadducees test Jesus by asking for a sign from heaven; he says they can interpret the appearance of the sky but not the signs of the times, and no sign will be given except the sign of Jonah.

16.title: The Leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees
16.context: Jesus warns the disciples to beware of the yeast of the Pharisees and Sadducees; they think he means bread, but he reminds them of the five and seven loaves, and they understand he means their teaching.

16.title: Peter’s Confession of Christ
16.context: At Caesarea Philippi Jesus asks who people say he is and who the disciples say he is; Peter answers that he is the Christ, the Son of the living God, and Jesus says the Father revealed this to him, that he will build his church on this rock, and gives him the keys of the kingdom.

16.title: Christ’s Passion Foretold
16.context: Jesus begins to tell the disciples he must suffer, be killed in Jerusalem and rise on the third day; Peter objects and is rebuked. Jesus says his followers must deny themselves and take up their cross, for gaining the world is worthless if one loses one’s life.

17.title: The Transfiguration
17.context: Jesus takes three disciples up a high mountain and is transfigured before them; Moses and Elijah appear, and a voice from the cloud says this is the beloved Son, listen to him. Coming down, Jesus says Elijah has already come, meaning John the Baptist.

17.title: The Boy with a Demon
17.context: A father begs Jesus to heal his son, who suffers seizures from a demon, because the disciples could not; Jesus rebukes the demon and the boy is healed, and he tells the disciples their faith was too small, for with faith like a mustard seed nothing would be impossible.

17.title: The Second Prediction of the Passion
17.context: In Galilee Jesus tells the disciples again that the Son of Man will be handed over and killed, and on the third day raised to life, and they are filled with grief.

17.title: The Temple Tax
17.context: At Capernaum the collectors of the temple tax ask Peter whether his teacher pays it; Jesus says the children are exempt, but so as not to cause offense he sends Peter to catch a fish, in whose mouth he finds a four-drachma coin to pay for both of them.

18.title: The Greatest in the Kingdom
18.context: The disciples ask who is greatest in the kingdom of heaven; Jesus places a little child among them and says unless they change and become like children they will never enter it, and whoever humbles himself like this child is the greatest.

18.title: Temptations and Trespasses
18.context: If anyone causes one of these little ones who believe in Jesus to stumble, it would be better for them to have a large millstone hung around their neck and be drowned; if your hand or foot causes you to stumble, cut it off — better to enter life maimed than be thrown into eternal fire.

18.title: The Parable of the Lost Sheep
18.context: See that you do not despise one of these little ones; if a man has a hundred sheep and one wanders away, he leaves the ninety-nine to look for the one that is lost — so your Father in heaven is not willing that any of these little ones should perish.

18.title: A Brother Who Sins
18.context: If a brother sins against you, first point it out privately, then take one or two others, and if he still refuses, tell the church; Jesus says what is bound or loosed on earth will be bound or loosed in heaven, and where two or three gather in his name he is among them.

18.title: The Unforgiving Servant
18.context: Peter asks whether forgiving seven times is enough, and Jesus says seventy-seven times, telling of a servant forgiven a huge debt who will not forgive a small one. The Father will treat those who do not forgive from the heart the same way.

19.title: Teachings about Divorce
19.context: Pharisees ask whether a man may divorce his wife for any reason; quoting Genesis, Jesus says God made them male and female to become one flesh, so what God has joined no one should separate. Moses allowed divorce because of hard hearts.

19.title: Jesus Blesses the Children
19.context: People bring little children for Jesus to lay hands on and pray for, and the disciples rebuke them, but Jesus says to let the children come and not hinder them, for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these, and he lays his hands on them.

19.title: The Rich Young Man
19.context: A rich young man asks how to gain eternal life; Jesus tells him to sell his possessions, give to the poor and follow him, and he leaves sad. Jesus says it is harder for the rich to enter God’s kingdom than for a camel to pass through a needle’s eye, but with God all things are possible.

20.title: The Parable of the Workers
20.context: The kingdom of heaven is like a landowner who hires workers at dawn and others later in the day, then pays them all the same wage; when the first complain, he says he has not wronged them and may be generous as he chooses — so the last will be first and the first last.

20.title: The Third Prediction of the Passion
20.context: On the way up to Jerusalem Jesus takes the twelve aside and tells them that the Son of Man will be delivered to the chief priests and scribes, condemned to death, handed over to the Gentiles to be mocked, flogged and crucified, and on the third day he will be raised to life.

20.title: A Mother’s Request
20.context: James and John’s mother asks that her sons sit at Jesus’ right and left in his kingdom; Jesus says whoever wants to be great must serve, for the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve and give his life as a ransom for many.

20.title: The Blind Men by the Road
20.context: As they leave Jericho, two blind men sitting by the roadside shout, “Lord, Son of David, have mercy on us!” Jesus has compassion and touches their eyes, and immediately they receive their sight and follow him.

21.title: The Triumphal Entry
21.context: Jesus sends two disciples for a donkey and her colt and rides into Jerusalem, fulfilling Zechariah’s prophecy; crowds spread cloaks and branches on the road shouting hosanna to the Son of David, blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, and the whole city asks who this is.

21.title: Jesus Cleanses the Temple
21.context: Jesus enters the temple, drives out the buyers and sellers and overturns the money changers’ tables, saying Scripture calls God’s house a house of prayer but they have made it a den of robbers; the blind and lame come to him and he heals them, while children shout hosanna in the temple.

21.title: The Barren Fig Tree
21.context: In the morning Jesus is hungry and finds a fig tree with leaves but no fruit; he says it will never bear fruit again and it withers at once; he tells the disciples that if they have faith and do not doubt, they will receive whatever they ask in prayer.

21.title: Jesus’ Authority Challenged
21.context: As Jesus teaches in the temple, the chief priests and elders demand by what authority he acts; he answers with a question about where John’s baptism came from — heaven or human origin? — and when they refuse to answer, he refuses to tell them.

21.title: The Parable of the Two Sons
21.context: A man asks his two sons to work in the vineyard; the first refuses but later changes his mind and goes, the second says yes but does not go. Jesus says tax collectors and prostitutes are entering the kingdom of God ahead of the leaders, because they believed John and the leaders did not.

21.title: The Parable of the Wicked Tenants
21.context: Jesus tells of a landowner who rents his vineyard to tenants who beat and kill the servants sent to collect the fruit and finally kill his son; quoting the psalm about the rejected stone becoming the cornerstone, he says the kingdom will be taken from them and given to a people who will produce its fruit.

22.title: The Parable of the Banquet
22.context: The kingdom is like a king’s wedding banquet for his son: the invited guests refuse to come and even kill his servants, so he gathers everyone from the streets, good and bad, but one guest without wedding clothes is thrown into the outer darkness; many are invited, but few are chosen.

22.title: Paying Taxes to Caesar
22.context: Pharisees and Herodians try to trap Jesus by asking whether it is right to pay taxes to Caesar; he asks for a coin, asks whose image and inscription it bears, and says to give Caesar what is Caesar’s and God what is God’s.

22.title: The Sadducees and the Resurrection
22.context: The Sadducees, who deny the resurrection, test Jesus with a woman married in turn to seven brothers; he says they are wrong because they know neither the Scriptures nor God’s power: in the resurrection people do not marry, and God is the God of the living, not the dead.

22.title: The Greatest Commandment
22.context: An expert in the law asks which commandment is greatest; Jesus answers that the first and greatest is to love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul and mind, and the second is to love your neighbor as yourself, and all the Law and the Prophets hang on these two.

22.title: Whose Son Is the Christ?
22.context: Jesus asks the Pharisees whose son the Christ is, and they answer David’s; quoting Psalm 110:1, he asks how David, speaking by the Spirit, can call him Lord if he is David’s son, and after that no one dares to ask him any more questions.

23.title: Woes to Scribes and Pharisees
23.context: Jesus says the scribes and Pharisees do not practice what they preach, so the people should heed their teaching but not copy their deeds; he pronounces a series of woes on their hypocrisy and their neglect of justice, mercy and faithfulness, like whitewashed tombs.

23.title: Lament over Jerusalem
23.context: Jesus laments over Jerusalem, which kills the prophets; how often he longed to gather her children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but they were unwilling, so their house will be left desolate until they say, blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.

24.title: Temple Destruction and Other Signs
24.context: As Jesus leaves the temple, his disciples point out its buildings, and he says not one stone will be left on another; on the Mount of Olives they ask privately when this will happen and what will be the sign of his coming and of the end of the age.

24.title: The Beginning of Birth Pains
24.context: The disciples ask when the temple will fall and what will signal his coming; Jesus says wars, famines, earthquakes and persecution are only the beginning of birth pains. They must not be deceived, those who endure to the end will be saved, and the gospel will be preached to all nations.

24.title: The Abomination of Desolation
24.context: Jesus says that when the abomination of desolation Daniel spoke of stands in the holy place, those in Judea should flee to the mountains; there will be great distress and false messiahs, but the Son of Man’s coming will be as unmistakable as lightning.

24.title: The Coming of the Son of Man
24.context: After that distress the heavens are shaken, the sign of the Son of Man appears, and all peoples will see him coming on the clouds with power and great glory; he will send his angels with a trumpet call to gather his elect.

24.title: The Lesson of the Fig Tree
